subtopic: INQUIRY INTO IRREGULARITIES AT POLLING STATION 50 OF ELECTORAL DISTRICT OF MELVILLE
INQUIRY INTO IRREGULARITIES AT POLLING STATION 50 OF ELECTORAL DISTRICT OF MELVILLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following representations that were made to the chief electoral officer by the

Hon. J. G. Gardiner, Minister of Agriculture, and Doctor Carlyle King, of Regina, acting president of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, Saskatchewan section, it was deemed advisable to institute an inquiry under section 70 of the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, into some irregularities which were revealed at the recount proceedings in connection with polling station No. 50 of the electoral district of Melville at the dominion elections of June 11 last.
On August 31, 1945, the chief justice of the court of king's bench of the province of Saskatchewan was appointed, pursuant to the above mentioned statutory provisions, to act as commissioner on the proposed inquiry. The inquiry was opened at Melville on Monday, October 9 last, and the taking of the evidence of the various witnesses lasted four days, from October 9 to October 12 inclusive. The report of the commissioner reached the chief electoral officer on the 19th instant.
I draw to the attention of the house the following conclusions of the commissioner's reiport. The first of these appears on page 29 of the report and reads as follows:
There are other features also which have a bearing on this issue and will be emphasized later in this report, and which serve also to support the conclusion which I have reached, namely that there were 71 ballots marked for Mr. Gardiner at this poll, and twenty-seven ballots for Mr. Benson, and that this count truly expressed the will of the 98 electors who voted at that poll.
I further find that although 12 of the Gardiner ballots had subsequently been tampered with by some person before the date of the recount that person was not Peter Cherneski or anyone who took part in the conduct of the poll. I am glad to state, and feel bound to state in the light of the evidence, and in fairness to these men, that there is no evidence whatever to support such a charge, but on the contrary there is convincing evidence of their innocence.
The second conclusion, appears at pages 27 and 28 of the report, and reads as follows:
The conclusion which forces itself upon me, and which I have reached after a most careful consideration of both documentary and oral evidence, is that the 12 ballots in question originally marked and counted for Mr. Gardiner were extracted from the envelope in which they were placed, while in Mr. Hunt's office; that they were then marked lightly for Mr. Benson and the marks immediately partly erased; that the unscrupulous person who perpetrated the fraud did so not only in order to invalidate these ballots in the recount but that the whole poll with its majority for Mr. Gardiner of 44 votes, might be thrown out and the will of the electors defeated. And let it be said that, from the criminal's point of view it would have the much-desired effect of defeating an outstanding member of the government of Canada a,nd an outstanding leader of the Liberal party in western Canada.

Elections-Irregularities
The third conclusion appears at page 29 of the report, and reads as follows:
The commission of the inquiry calls upon me to inquire in particular . . whether any ballots were marked or defaced subsequent to their being deposited in the ballot boxes on polling day and, if so, to ascertain the person or persons responsible therefor."
I have at great length tried to answer that question, but if it be desirable that I should answer with brevity, my answer to the first part of the question is "yes, unquestionably," and as to the second part of the question, my answer is. "I have not been able to ascertain, and have not the slightest idea as to the identity of the person or persons responsible therefor."
Mr. Speaker, I now lay on the table of the house the commissioner's report of the Melville inquiry. This report was reecived by the chief electoral officer on the 19th instant.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
subtopic: INQUIRY INTO IRREGULARITIES AT POLLING STATION 50 OF ELECTORAL DISTRICT OF MELVILLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose at a time such as this, one who is concerned and who has reason to welcome the report should be most magnanimous with those who have been responsible for the necessity for making the report: But I think as a question of privilege, and in the light of the report made by the chief electoral officer, I should call attention to certain statements made reflecting upon my actions as a candidate in the election held on June 11 last, and questioning my right to sit as a member of this house.
On the night of the election my majority was reported to be 554. The official count was made on June 19, when it was reported that through correction of polls between the count on election night, and as a result of the soldier vote, the majority was reduced to 32. The CXJ.F. candidate, Mr. Benson, asked for a recount, and rumours were circulated that this majority could be wiped out through the fact that persons voted who had no right to vote. That recount was held beginning July 16, 1945.
During the recount no irregularities bearing upon the result of the election were discovered except at poll 50. I immediately asked that the chief electoral officer investigate and report. He has now reported, and a copy of his report has been tabled. This report is based upon the findings of Chief Justice Brown of the court of king's bench in Saskatchewan, who was appointed to investigate rumours being circulated to the effect that officials at poll 50 had tampered with the ballots on election day, possibly during the lunch hour when the poll was closed for an hour at the request of the C.C.F. scrutineer, in order that he might go home for lunch and bring his wife to vote. The finding of the judge is that no such tampering with the ballots took place, and that the poll officials were innocent of the charges.
Having listened to the representations of those who conducted the recount on their behalf, and having reviewed all the evidence gathered by an exhaustive search upon which to upset the election, under the Controverted Elections Act, the CbC.F. provincial executive held a meeting in Regina, after which an announcement was made in the Regina Leader of August 30, 1945, by Doctor Carlyle King, acting president. That announcement was as follows:
Since the recount the C.C.F. has been considering taking action under the Controverted Elections Act, as an investigation by the party suggested there was an irregularity in the conducting of the balloting at poll 50 in the riding.
Doctor King said further:
Although our investigations in recent weeks have brought to light many irregularities in the holding of the election on June 11, the legal loopholes in the Controverted Elections Act make it unwise for us to risk the thousands of dollars which an appeal under the act would cost.
He added that the C;C.F. eagerly awaits the chief electoral officer's promised inquiry into the conduct of the balloting at poll 50, and stated further:
At that inquiry we will be prepared to present evidence that will show that Mr. Gardiner has no right to the Melville seat.
Chief Justice Brown began his investigations under instructions from the chief electoral officer on October 9, 1945 and made his report November 17. The chief electoral officer made his report to-day. The finding is the reverse of what the C.C.F. claimed they would show. In my opinion the president of the C.C.F. should withdraw the entire charge, which of course in the light of Jhe evidence has been proven to be an untrue charge.
But as a matter of privilege what I desired to draw particularly to the attention of the house was this. The hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) is reported in the press of October 29 to have said at Hamilton on October 28:
Even as late as this summer there was dirty work at the polls in Saskatchewan. I maintain that Mr. Gardiner had no right to sit in the House of Commons. We did not have the money to carry it through, but it was proved that ballots had been tampered with.
I need hardly call attention to the impropriety of a member of this house making such a statement, even if it were eventually found to be true, at the very time an investigation concurred in by his party was being held. But since its claims have been found to reflect upon my opponents rather than upon me, the statement is doubly reprehensible.
The hon. member for Yorkton apparently felt he had stated the case a little strongly)
Elections-Irregularities

because when I was leaving the house on the evening of October 29 a page boy rushed to me in the corridor with a note. I read it when I reached my office. In the first place I wish to state that if he had desired to withdraw or correct anything appearing in the press he should have done so on the floor of the house publicly. But I do not wonder that he sent this message in the manner he did. It reads as follows:
October 29
Mr. Gardiner:
The Globe and Mail carries a very irresponsible report of my statement in Hamilton. I never said anything about fraud.
Legally and technically your seat in the house cannot be challenged. No statement of mine could have been construed otherwise.
Sincerely,	.
G. H. Castleden.
The only denial registered in this note is that he used the word "fraud". The report in the Globe and Mail does not state that the hon. member for Yorkton used the word "fraud". The heading reads: "Says Gardiner elected through ballot fraud." What was declared by the hon. member for Yorkton and other party members to have happened in Melville certainly would have constituted ballot fraud if it had occurred. If it had been found that twelve ballots originally marked for Benson had been removed from the envelope containing Benson's ballots, the cross marked opposite my name and the ballots deposited in the envelope containing my ballots, which was contended, I certainly should have considered that an attempt had been made to defraud the electors to my advantage, and should have felt called upon to resign my seat. [DOT]
The judge finds that such a thing did not and could not have happened under the circumstances. He finds that there was an attempt made to defraud the electors, and he actually uses the word "fraud". He states this was done by taking twelve ballots from the envelope containing the ballots marked for me, marking [DOT] an "X" opposite Benson's name, rubbing it off, and putting the ballots back in the envelope containing my ballots, from which they had been removed, in an effort to upset the whole poll, where I had a majority of forty-four, and thus elect my opponent at the recount. As a matter of fact that was asked for at the recount.
In my opinion the word "fraud" properly defines what the hon. member for Yorkton charged and properly describes what the judge reports some criminal attempted to do. He very definitely finds that this crime was not % 
committed by any of the officials at poll No. 50, but by some one who wished to injure me and, through me, the Liberal party.
The	hon. member	for	Yorkton has	notdenied	his statement	at	Hamilton; he	hasmerely	stated that "legally and technically"my seat in the house cannot be challenged. I would ask him publicly to withdraw the statement made at Hamilton and to admit that legally, technically, morally and in every way I am entitled to sit as a member of this house	representing	the	constituency	of
Melville.
I sat through the recount at Melville and helped check every ballot. I am sure I can say without any fear of contradiction by anyone who did likewise that all the parties were agreed that apart from poll No. 50 no criticism could be made of the conduct of the polls in that election. The highest possible praise is due those who took the soldiers' vote, even though I did not get a majority of their votes.
In view of the fact that there were only a few constituencies checked following that vote I think hon. members would expect me to say that I sat as one of those who were making the recount and we checked the ballots polled for the whole constituency. After they had been checked, there were only fourteen ballots that were questioned by anyone, and those fourteen were questioned only on the ground that the men who had cast the ballots had given their addresses as points outside the constituency. All but four of those points were so close to the boundaries of the constituency that it was apparent to everyone that those ten men possibly lived inside the seat but had post office addresses outside the constituency. That was found to be the case.
I want to say that it is to the credit of the officers who conducted the vote of the overseas men, and it is to the credit of the overseas men themselves, that although a vote could be cast over an area extending from that constituency east and west for thousands of miles, when the votes were brought back and recounted nothing could be found which was detrimental to those who had conducted that election in that particular way.
The judge has now found that even poll No. 50 was conducted in a manner which gave a correct expression of the intent of the voters. Therefore I think I am justified in saying that the whole election was conducted in a proper manner.
There was one question which was raised and which I think should be mentioned. It was contended at one stage that a sufficient number of Indians had voted to make it possible to

Elections-Irregularities
upset the election if their rotes were disallowed. In other words, it was contended) that those votes, along with some others, might have made a total of thirty-two, and if thirty-two Indian votes had been cast, then the election might be upset. This was to my personal knowledge investigated by both the Liberals and the C.C.E., and I presume they found what we found, namely first, that there were not enough Indian votes to change the results of the election, even if they had all been cast for me and been disallowed. Second, it was found that as many Indians were brought to the polls by C.C.F. workers as by Liberals. Third, these particular Indians are the wives of returhed men of the first great war, and have been voting with their husbands ever since the last war without objection, on [DOT] the part of anyone. I think that will be agreed to by everyone. I think if we denied them the vote it would be deeply resented by all their friends of every party. So the matter was dropped. In my opinion the elections act should be amended to give them the legal right to vote. These women in the west-I do not know about the east-have been, voting in both provincial and, federal elections. They come to the polls with their husbands, and to my knowledge no one has ever objected seriously to their voting. They did vote on this occasion, but there were not enough of them to make a difference in the election, no matter how they voted.
There were n.o other irregularities that were even rumoured, to my knowledge. Therefore, I submit that it was not a lack of funds but a lack of evidence to substantiate reckless, unscrupulous and untrue charges which caused the C.C.F. to decide not to take action under the Controverted Elections Act. If they wish to have the respect of reasonable people I think they should be chivalrous enough to say so I think the election was properly conducted, and while the majority was not as great as I should have liked to have it, I am sure that they have done sufficient to assure that it will be greater the next time.

Mr. MITCHELL':

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TRANSFER OF SURPLUS NAVAL VESSELS TO NAVY LEAGUE
speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough to give me notice of this question. The transfer of surplus naval craft to the Navy League of Canada for the use of the sea cadets for training has been given considerable thought. A number of small craft such as sailing boats and harbour craft are made available for use by the sea cadets, but with respect to the heavier type of naval craft it has been felt advisable to keep these for the Royal Canadian Naval divisions, where they would be available for training purposes, not only for sea cadets but also for the naval reserve forces. I understand that these larger craft are also made available for the sea cadet camps which are in operation during the summer and provision is also made whereby a number of these cadets are taken out for training cruises on fairly large training vessels in the great lakes and at other points. I have no doubt that that practice will be continued.

I think that if the hon. member for Kootenay West speaks now he should not speak for more than ten minutes.

I shall not occupy more than a few minutes, Mr. Chairman. I was merely going to make a few remarks by way of proposals to the government as aids to a solution of the Japanese question: I assure you I shall not detain the committee long.
First, send back all Japanese of proven disloyalty as soon as possible to Japan. We do not for one minute defend any person who has been disloyal to this country.
Second, in connection with this question of repatriation-and I do hope the minister will give serious consideration to this-that a tribunal be appointed, including at least one representative of the Christian churches, with a thorough knowledge of Japanese, to consider applications for a change of decision in connection with declarations formerly made in the matter of repatriation. I ask the minister, I almost plead with him, to do that, because while I freely admit that there was no coercion in the accepted sense of the word, these declarations were signed under circumstances which were certainly not normal, and I believe these people's cases should be reviewed in the manner I suggest.
Third, while I know that this question of enemy alien property does not come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour, I ask him to use his good influence and the knowledge he has of this situation to promote an immediate iinvestigation of the assets disposed of through the custodian of enemy alien property, and complete restitution in respect of all injustices proven in this connection. I may say that there are thousands of citizens in

British Columbia of all political parties who believe that great injustice has been done in this matter.
Fourth, I would suggest it would be good policy for the Department of Labour and this government to give widespread publicity to the part which people of Japanese origin have played in the war effort in this country, including the purchase of victory bonds, subscriptions to the Red Cross, vital work in the lumber industry-the minister has mentioned the sugar beet industry-and enlistments in the Canadian army.
Fifth, I would suggest that the minister remove a frequent cause of opposition to these oriental groups in this country by seeing that legislation is passed at the first opportunity which will assure fair employment practices throughout this dominion.
Sixth, I suggest that the minister enlist the support of organizations and people throughout this country in educational campaigns to develop a high appreciation and understanding of this important problem, one of the many problems which have to be solved if democracy is to function in this country.
Before concluding, I wish to pay a tribute to the churches of all faiths and to a wide section of the press for the splendid stand they have taken against racial discrimination-in brief, for the stand they have taken against the very seeds of nazism.
These suggestions, Mr. Chairman, I put forward as suggestions to be given effect to by the government; but every Canadian has a duty to perform in this connection, and it is to combat racialism with all his heart, with all his mind, and with all his strength, because I am quite sure that the flower of democracy cannot come to fruition so long as this evil, what I would term this syphilis of the ;spirit, is destroyed and no longer exists in this country.

Mr. Chairman, in regard to this Japanese question I can only give my own experiences. No sooner was war declared than we as farmers were asked to produce to capacity. Food was needed1, and we had no help with which to produce food. The only help that I could see available were Japanese who were then in, I assume, concentration and working camps, or being transported from British Columbia to various parts of Canada.

May I say to my hon. friend that there are comparatively few in concentration camps; if I am correctly informed, at the moment there are about four hundred. I would not like it to go abroad* that all the 47696-152i
Demobilization-Labour
Japanese in this country are in concentration camps. I am sure my hon. friend will agree with me.

Yes; I too would want that clearly understood. I made every effort to obtain Japanese, and with considerable expense and trouble I finally obtained one, who -was recommended to me, to work on the farm. He was a married man with several children. We provided him with a cottage and everything which should be provided on a good ' farm. It was not very long, however, before this man in my presence pointed to our own training planes flying overhead and said, "Japanese better." I heard his children in our own yard singing "Hong Kong Singapore, Hong Kong Singapore." This man came to me in my own home and1 told me that while he was in the camp at Jasper these Japanese had secretly manufactured knives, some of them long, thin, slender knives, from bits of saws and* so on, so that, as far as I understood him, practically all of them were armed. I could mention many other instances, but I will not take up the time of the committee. At any rate, this man was certainly not interested in Canada or in producing food. I thought however that if he had another Japanese as a companion he might settle down and be of value to us. I was approached*- I did not take the initiative-by a Japanese young lady who was going to the university of ALberta. She told me that her father, an expert poultryman and market gardener, was anxious to come to Alberta and get on a farm, that he did not like it where he was, and if I would provide him with a cottage- I had three empty cottages on the farm-he would come there with his wife and his nineteen-year-old son and together they would take over the poultry and* gardening end of the farm and* help in the production of foodstuffs generally.	.
I went to considerable trouble and finally brought this family to my farm; personally hauled all their belongings to the farm, and provided them with a cottage. I settled them. What happened? This nineteen-year-old boy disappeared. He was a husky lad, too, for he had been brought up in Canada. I was left alone without any help. I called my own son, who is with me to-day and who is listening to me. I took him out of school to go and work on* the farm to take the place of that man, because our other man had left to join the armed forces. Yes, I took my own son out of school, and lie has never been able to return; he has worked on that farm and produced for all he was worth, and for the first time since 1938 is this boy having a
Demobilization-Labour

holiday. He has worked every day, Sundays and Christmas day included, serving his country.
And where was this nineteen-year-old Japanese boy? I did not know. I asked his father, and he made certain gestures indicating that he did not know. Finally I got on the boy's track and I discovered that he was living with his sisters in the city of Edmonton, attending high school there, though that had been refused my own daughter because we did not live in that particular district. My own daughter had to go to Leduc, about ten miles south; yet here was this Japanese boy actually going to school in Edmonlton, while my own son, who should have been in school, was working on the farm. Did I receive help from these Japanese? Not at all. My own son was appealed to by these Japanese on Sundays to help them when the snow came to get their, wood in so that they could be kept warm. They did not even go into the bush to obtain fuel when they had an opportunity 'before the snow came.
I do not need to spend any more time on that. I will not attack the Minister of Labour, and I hope that I shall not embarrass him in any way, because he has his hands full of labour troubles. His road is chosen for him by the government, and I know it is a hard one to travel, twisting and turning here and there with mud holes all over the place. That is why this old jalopy is stuck now with this strike at the Ford plant.
What has happened? Here are men who have broken out of the pasture, as it were- broken out of the pen. What will you do about it? Let us take a walk out to my farm, because I have such strikes constantly if I am not on the job. To give you an illustration of how we common farmers would deal with such a problem, let us use our imaginations for a few moments. We will imagine we' are on my farm and the hogs have broken out of the pen. I am standing in the kitchen waiting for a couple of doughnuts to cool off, because my wife happens to be frying them, and looking through the window I see the hogs rooting in the kitchen garden. What would this parliament do under such circumstances? I am afraid it would debate the subject. It would1 make lengthy and perhaps brilliant speeches on nothing at all-because I have sat here for weeks biting my fingernails and wondering when we would get down to business. But what would I do under the circumstances? I would go to my wife and kiss her on the'cheek and she would stand back, place her hands on her hips, look me up and down, and say "Now, what do

you want?" And I would say, "My love, look out the window at nature's marvels", and then I would dodge the broom as she grabbed it and rushed out the back door taking the screen with her. The hogs would scatter in all directions; but where am I?

In the kitchen eating
doughnuts.

You will find me, sir, in the hog pen, sitting there on an upturned swill pail, my elbows on my knees, my face in my hands, trying to think like a hog. I say trying to think like a hog; and I want you to remember this, because a pig, if not influenced by unnatural conditions, always thinks right. In other words, the mind of animals, not polluted by man-made rules and regulations and all the rest of it, always thinks as nature compels it to think. These hogs broke out of the pen because I, who have taken upon myself supreme authority over them, as it were, have imposed conditions upon them that compel them to get out of that pen. It is therefore up to me to find out what it is that has driven these hogs out of the pen.
Now let us look at these- men. After I discovered what it was that the animals needed and wanted, I had to give them, of- course, those wants at the earliest possible moment so as to get them back into the pen. Let us take the workers at the Ford plant. What do they want? An increase in pay perhaps. I can assure them right now that they will never get it from the Ford plant.
Does the hon. member consider these workers pigs?

I consider these workers
mentally far superior to many who imagine they are superior to them. I use that as an illustration. These men want certain results, and I was trying to illustrate what they want. If they are not influenced by agitators they can easily demonstrate what they want. I said before that the Ford1 plant cannot give increases in wages unless they pay lees for their raw materials; and if they do that the steel workers are going to strike. It is an utter impossibility for the Ford plant to pay less for their raw products. They cannot pay any less wages to their foremen, their managers or the managing directors and so on, because if they do, those men will just quit working for the firm and go elsewhere. They cannot cut down on the interest paid to those who have invested their savings and their earnings in this business, and from which they deserve a just reward. I do not think anyone is receiving too high a rate of interest on those investments. There is only one other way in which the Ford plant

Demobilization-Labour
can possibly1 obtain money with which to pay these men higher wages, and that it to increase the price of their products to the consumers. You andi I and all the rest of us are consumers. We would pay ourselves. It is very similar to this racket called "compulsory contributory unemployment insurance," which is nothing but a farce. For example, the worker pays one-third, the firm for which he works pays one-third and the government pay's one-third.

I would say that if the Ford company had received $17,000,000 profit it would be a mighty good thing. I know that if they' made that profit they would immediately' erect another factory and therefore employ more men. That is their business, not mine. [DOT]
To go on with the compulsory contributory unemployment insurance that I was speaking of, the men pay one-third, the firm pays one-third and the government pays one-third. It is taken from them. They' have no option; they are forced to contribute this amount. Where does the firm get its third? It gets it by merely increasing the price to the consumers, and we as consumers have to pay that one-third also. Where does the government get its one-third? It taxes it out of our pockets, and we pay that third; therefore we pay it all.
These men desire something; they are working for something. They go to work in this factory, or in any factory, we will say, at the age of eighteen or twenty. They want to get a job; they want to earn a living. They are willing and anxious to get work to earn a living. Working is a means to an end. Therefore they go to work possibly on Monday morning, and they will work hour after hour all day on Monday. They will work again all day Tuesday and Wednesday and Thursday and Friday, and by Saturday they are getting a little tired. But the next Monday they must go to work again. In other words they will work hour after hour, day after day, week after week, and month after month, for as long as five years. At the end of that time perhaps they may say, "Well, we can begin to live now,"-but no; they have to get to work again as soon as the little holiday is over. They start all over again and they work again year after year for another five years, or ten or more years. They will work until they are forty or forty-five years old, and still they cannot retire and
enjoy life-for that is what they want. That is why they work-to be able to enjoy life, to be able to live. Yet they must keep on working until they are forty-five years of age, until they are fifty, until they are fifty-five, until they are sixty, sixty-five, even up to seventy years of age, and then we give them a small pittance of $30 a month. Imagine!
What is the solution? Well, the first thing is to cut out all this taxation, abolish taxes on incomes of $5,000 a year and less. That would enable them to live a little bit of the time anyway. Next cut down gradually all taxation on all goods offered for sale, and when we have that abolished begin to pay a rightful dividend which will bring up the purchasing power of the people so that they may be able to purchase the goods that they produce in association.

I have asked for a few minutes because I have something to say. First I would congratulate the minister, his deputy and his staff upon the work they have done during past years. I think I was the first or perhaps the only member who, when I occupied a seat on the other side, stood in my place and championed the cause of the minister because of his record as a workman and an executive helper. You cannot write to the Department of Labour to-day without getting an answer, whether you get what you ask foT or not. I hope that that will continue.
In my statement at that time I spoke of his character, and his record has been carried out by his statement when he said that it is necessary for labour and capital to walk the same road. That shows that he is getting pretty close to the programme of the Master Carpenter of Nazareth when he said:
And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain.
I do not like strikes, but I know that in industry a strike is just as important as an operation on the human body. Sometimes disease gets into the human body and it is necessary for a specialist to come along and see that an operation is performed. But an operation on the human body always hurts, and it leaves a weakness afterwards. A strike is caused in industry when some disease creeps in and something gets wrong. I think a strike is absolutely necessary in order to clear away something that hurts the people who are operating that place.
I was in Winnipeg on Saturday and I found a strike of this type going on. I found the Free Press and the Tribune were trying to get out a paper but there was no advertising in it and therefore it was not paying. I went
Demobilization-Labour

into a big store and I wondered why it was that the people knew when there was a big sale on. The rush was just as large as ever. I asked somebody why it was, and he said, "Well, it comes over the radio." Therefore the papers are hurting themselves; the management are hurting themselves and the workers are hurting themselves because they are going to lose a good deal in that way. I think the workers must have the right to strike. I should like to ask the Minister of Labour why it is that some unions in Canada get along without striking and others are continually at it. Take the running trades. The late member for Kenora stood up in this house and said: "We can get along by collaborating, by discussing our problems with the officials." It is better for them to get along without a strike if they can do it, but sometimes a strike is necessary. I know I was sick at heart last night when I heard over the radio that the Ford) strike was not settled. I think it ought to- have been settled. I agree with the Minister of Reconstruction that while the men may have ma.de some mistakes and the leaders of labour have made some mistakes, yet tire Ford people and management themselves are more responsible. I can remember the first time when I owned a Ford car, and was mighty proud of it; because Henry Ford had fitted out a peace ship to go across the Atlantic to tell the German leaders and others that the peace of the world should be maintained. I would tell the descendants of Henry Ford to-day, from my place in the house, that before we can have peace outside we have to have peace at home, and' that they should get busy and settle their own differences with their own workers- because those workers are surely reasonable. I want a Ford car-yes; but I do not care whether I ride in it or not. I would just as soon have a baby Austin, any time.
How is the Minister of Reconstruction going to get on with his programme? How is he going to make a success of his plan for reconstruction if management and labour do not get together? During the last session the bankers' association were on the carpet. It was shown that the white-collared workers in the banks to-day are treated a little better than they were in years gone by, when a young man would start to work in a bank for $400 a year. It was known then, as it is known to-day, that a dollar earned in a bank will not buy any more boots or clothes than a dollar earned by driving a model-T Ford in the city of Ottawa.
The bankers have been doing considerably better, and that is a point which gives us some hope. But why is it that a banker must

spend long hours and not receive anything nearly the amount of pay received by, we will say, a paper maker? One receives $2 an hour, and the other does not receive much more than $2 or $3 a day. Why? It is because of organization. The white-collared workers should get busy and organize. I realize that some tribute must be paid to the bankers, because I have learned that when the young men have come back from the war, to the banks, their increases in wages have continued, just as if they had been working right along. While the banks are not paying what we think they should pay, we must give them their due.
Let me say one word about the Japanese. Perhaps it may be suggested that I have no right to speak on -this subject. But I have. The government has no right to tell British Columbia that it must take the Japanese and have them segregated there. British Columbia has no greater responsibility than any other province to supply homes to those who have come out from Japan, and their descendants. But Canadian citizenship is a sacred thing; whether a man be Japanese, Indian or Irish, his citizenship is his sacred right, and we must be careful how we handle it.
In the three minutes of my time remaining I shall speak only briefly about the union shop. My experience is that it works, and it would be in' the best interests of the Ford Motor company if they adopted the union-shop immediately. I am sure if -the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe were in his seat he would support me in what I am saying. Any company that has operated under this arrangement does not want to return to any other. The superintendent of the Great Lakes Pulp and Paper company, of which the hon. member is president, would have nothing but the union shop, because it does away with union activities in working hours, and with drives for membership. Men and management work happily together. We have in Fort William a concern in which the union shop Operates, and I have been told by the superintendent and manager of the plant that he would not go back to the old way.
The union shop makes contented workers; when a man is a member of a union he knows what lhe has to pay. The cure for the troubles between capital and labour to-day is not only collective bargaining, although it may help; the cure will be effected only when leaders and workmen adopt the rule laid down by the Master Workman of Galilee, that each Shall help the other to carry his burden.

Demobilization-Labour

The hon. member for Fort William has said that Canadian citizenship is a sacred thing. I agree with that. But always remember this, that when this nation gives citizenship to an individual from another country, that citizenship carries with it certain obligations. Let that sink in.
I have said before in this chamber that you do not build a nation or an empire by sitting on the fence. It has been the courage of the people that has ma.de this country what it is, the courage of those who fought against the enemy in this and in the last war. I know the desperate position in which the British people found themselves in 1942. That was when we stood alone; that was when we needed friends, and the cooperation of persons who had taken o'ut citizenship in this country.
What do we find? What has been our record in the past? Up until the defeat of Japan the Japanese wanted to go back to their own country. As I said yesterday, this is a free country, and we took them at their word. But when the atomic bomb cropped up, and Japan was defeated, they were prepared to change their minds. That is the position in a nutshell.
I have no objection to sitting here for the next two or three weeks-but I am dreaming of a white Christmas. I know most hon. members are like myself, and that if they wished to do so they could condense their basic arguments into brief speeches. I have no right to stand in the way of criticism of my department, because the right to differ in -opinion is the basis of human freedom. But let us get on with the washing; let us make sure that my good western friend-and I see the hon. member for Cariboo smiling at me- -has an opportunity to get a seat on the train so that he may go home to see his wife and children.

I do not rise at this time to criticize. When I speak in the house it is to . provoke thought on the part of those who have responsibilities, when I think they are slipping up. If I succeed in leaving some thought with them, I may do my share toward helping to correct conditions which perhaps are not handled as they should be.
On many occasions in this chamber I have said that in my view the Department of Labour was the most important department in the government during the process of fighting the war. Anyone who has watched the activities of that department must agree with me. The same is true in this time of reconversion.
If anyone cares, to look at the minister's estimates he will find there are twenty-two items, running into large sums of money and reaching into every aspect of the economy of our country. The job of taking servicemen out of the services, training them, finding employment for them and looking after them when they are unemployed is that of the Minister of Labour. I listened to his statement last night and I read it again to-day. It was a most informative statement. He gave many facts and figures. Sometimes figures may be misleading, and I am going to say a few words on that.
I am not going to talk about the Japanese question, because there are other hon. members more expert on that than I am. That matter is now in the hands of the Department of Labour; it is a government responsibility. We have expressed our opinion as to the rights of citizenship; our position is clear; the mechanics of working out the problem' is the responsibility of the government, and1 I am not going to delve into them.
I want to say just a few words on the question of union security. Last night the hon. member for Calgary West made an honest attempt to find a solution to conciliation and other problems. While I do not wholly a'gree with him, I do think that he tried honestly to offer us something. This question of union security is going to bother the Department of Labour more than any other question that will come before it in the next year or two, and an endeavour should be made now to find some means of answering it.
Many people talk very loosely about union security. Many of them have no conception of what they want when they refer to union security. I think the greatest difficulty facing many people is that of defining exactly what they want. But that has never bothered me very much. All the collective security that I want is a collective bargaining act in the province in which you are attempting to establish union security. That is the first thing that should be done. Second, if a majority of the workers are satisfied with a certain union the collective bargaining machinery in the province should * make it mandatory that there be a revocable check-off set up. I do not want to harness any one in an organization without the right of backing out if he so desires. Lf a union has a check-off on a volunatry basis, where the member places his card in the office with the right to pull out that card if he so desires, that is all the union security that I think is necessary. If an organization set up for the purpose of bargaining collectively with the employer justi-

Demobilization-Labour
fies its existence, if it is doing the kind of job it should do for its membership, it should have no fear of its membership leaving the organization. That is not too much to ask. I think that is all the machinery that is necessary.
My experience, and I think it is the experience of many others, over the past thirty years is that when you harness the membership of an organization so that they cannot back out if they so desire there is a tendency to create a dictatorship or bureaucracy. The men are anchored and they must stay whether they like it or not. It should be clearly understood that a revocable check-off is all that is necessary. Once that is set up, an organization should be able to hold on the basis of service to its membership. The mine" workers are pretty tough people. We have been unionized for the last thirty years. We have that kind of arrangement, and I know it works. There is no danger in union security if you have a proper trade union act in the province.
In dealing last night with the matter of conciliation the hon. member for Calgary West put his finger on the sore spot. You may have an unanimous decision of a conciliation board, but there is no way of enforcing it. Once a decision is given, you have nowhere to go. If it is acceptable to the union, it is fine; if it is not, you still have a dispute on your hands. He suggested the possibility of handing over the rights of a referee to supreme court judges to be selected by the Minister of Justice.
I know that there has to be some end to these things, but I also know that if the government enacts legislation that places the final, say in labour disputes in the hands of the judiciary, you will have an immediate uprising from one end of the country to the other. It would be looked upon as compulsory arbitration, because the decisions would be made from the legalistic rather than the economic point of view.
It was tried in 1918.

It was tried and the reaction was completely against it. In the first analysis we must set up proper labour legislation in each of our provinces. It must be done provincially, because the British North America Act prevents you from doing it nationally. If you have trade union acts such as you have in most of the provinces across this country, if the majority of your industrial workers are bargaining collectively with their employers, then I think you will eliminate the great majority of your disputes.
For example, in the mine workers' union an umpire is selected by the operating company and by the union. His salary is paid on a
(Mr. Gillis.l	.
fifty-fifty basis by the union and the company. They have difficulty sometimes in getting the proper man, but where disputes arise during the term of the contract-once your contract is signed a lot of your difficulties are over- they are referred to the referee. His job is to interpret the contract and take care of any disputes that arise.
Is that a permanent position, or is the hon. member referring to what we call an independent chairman w7ho is appointed for each dispute?

No, he is a permanent
appointee.
We have not that. Our independent chairman is paid on a fifty-fifty basis, but I see there is a distinction.

This is the permanent official, and he is paid on a fifty-fifty basis by the union and the coal company. He maintains an office and has a full-time job. He studies the contract, he meets with the people, and he knows the dispute pretty thoroughly. He is carefully selected, and his judgment is accepted. I have never known one of his judgments to be disputed by either side.
What would his salary be?

Not so much-probably
around $3,500 a year. In that way most of the disputes are kept out of the field of conciliation. If we could establish collective bargaining acts provincially, if union agreements could be signed with the operators, if we could set up umpire machinery to interpret the terms of the agreements and handle the grievances as they arise, we would do much to keep disputes out of the national field.
How large an area does that scheme cover?
It covers 12,000 miners.
In one province?

Partly New Brunswick, but mostly in Nova Scotia. It is all contingent upon the establishment of proper collective bargaining machinery.
The dominion-provincial conference is to take place pretty soon. The dominion proposals to the provinces in the field of collective bargaining assure us that this matter is on the agenda. I should like to leave this thought with the minister. We are going to have to do one of two things. We are in an age when working people realize that democracy in industry is necessary, and without the kind of machinery we have been talking about you have not industrial democracy. The thing

Demobilization-Labour
is all one-sided when the 'boss can sit in his office and dictate to you; that is dictatorship, not democracy. There will have to be a thorough understanding on this matter. Either something must be done in every province to provide collective bargaining legislation which is uniform, or the dominion government will have to ask the provinces to relinquish their rights in this field, and the national labour code must be expanded into collective bargaining legislation which will be uniform from one end of the dominion to the other.
When the McTague commission were taking the evidence upon which the present code is based the horn, member for Vancouver East and myself had the privilege of appearing before that commission and presenting a brief. When we were told that, the purpose was merely to establish a code under the War Measures Act, and that it would last only for the duration of the war, I told the chairman that I would not be very much interested in giving evidence. If it is only a makeshift, something which is to be thrown, overboard When the war is over, you are wasting your time and the time of the people who assemble this evidence and appear before the commission. If the British North America Act is in, the way, we can change it. Definitely it is a controversial problem. But if it was necessary to lay down a code during the war, we should have made a good job of it: we should have enacted a national labour code in agreement with the provinces which would have been working to-day.
The dominion-provincial conference should have a thorough understanding about this matter. We ini Nova Scotia are not so badly off as regards trade union legislation. But when the Minister of Labour for Nova Scotia was speaking to the McTague commission he definitely stated that he and the government he represented were quite prepared to have the subject dealt with nationally,. In order that a code which would establish uniformity across the country could be laid down they were prepared to relinquish their rights in that field in favour of the dominion government. I am told that it is on the agenda, and I hope that by the time the conference is over we shall have something worth while.
I should like to be clear on this point: are there any federal government proposals to the provincial governments? I understand there are none.

Only last night I checked up
on the dominion proposals to the dominion-provincial conference, and collective bargaining is definitely included. They do not make any specific proposals, but the matter is on the
agenda and it will be discussed, and there is no doubt that some of the provinces will have something definite to say about it. I think all the evidence necessary to determine this question was assembled1 by the McTague commission. There should not be any guessing about it, because the general public, organized labour, anybody who had anything to say on the subject, went in and made presentations, and there is a comprehensive set-up available to-day.
Another thought. I should like to leave with the minister is this. He may say that this matter, comes under the Department of. Munitions and Supply. But these departments today are all interlocked!-finance, labour, munitions and supply, reconstruction. They all dovetail into this one problem, of employment and training, because there is a financial problem, a reconversion problem, and the problem of the minister in putting men to work. The finance department can,, employ them, the Minister of Reconstruction can throw out a few thousand people, but the Minister of Labour has to find work for them. So all the departments are tied together in this respect.
As the minister knows, the employment problem in Nova Scotia from one end of the province to the other is very serious. To-day a coal commission is sitting to examine into the problem. It may be a few months before it is in a position to report. The problem is a national one. If there is one industry in Canada about which the federal government is going to have to do something it is the coal industry. The right to the resources is, of course, in the hands of the province. But the federal government has been pouring millions of dollars into the industry, and continues to do it; otherwise it would collapse. When this royal commission reports, one of its most important duties will be to lay down a national fuel policy so that that resource will be utilized to its maximum, and the maximum return obtained from the industry for the money the government puts into it. But when [DOT] that commission makes its report it will not be in, a position to lay down a national fuel policy, because again you are up against provincial jurisdiction, and in checking over the dominion proposals to the dominion-provincial conference I find that that is not on the agenda. I suggest that, whoever may represent the dominion government at the conference, the question of a national fuel policy and the functions of this commission should be discussed, and if it is necessary for the federal government to act as a crutch for the rest of our natural life for the coal industry
Demobilization-Labour

of this province, if they have to finance and stand behind it, they should have a lot to say as to its management. You are not going to be able to say anything as to its management until such time as you have an understanding with the province on it. Personally I am convinced, and have been for some time, that it is a national industry which will have to be taken over sooner or later; because, looking at the figures of subsidies and so forth during the war period, it seems clear that any industry which has to be sustained from the public treasury to the extent to which the coal industry has been sustained should undergo, a certain amount of public supervision through the government. I leave that thought with the minister, because I believe the matter will have to be discussed at the dominiomprovineial conference.
Then there is the matter of employment. Figures are misleading, as I said a few minutes ago, and certainly they are misleading in the matter of employment. I had some considerable correspondence with the Minister of Munitions and Supply on this business; and you will find that even your selective service figures from the officers will mislead you. For example, one report I had, and I went to the office for it, showed that in the Sydney area there were 564 applications, whereas the number of vacancies listed was 693. That would lead one to believe that there were more jobs available in that community than there were applicants. But I say that is misleading because 493 of those vacancies were for first-class coal miners, and all the vacancies which could be filled by .local applicants numbered 71. The people listed for employment could do light work; they might work around the surface, they could go at datal work and around the mines. But that kind of employment was not available, and men physically and otherwise qualified as miners were not there.
The thought I should like to leave with the minister is based on a serious situation, which I checked up while I was home. I went to the coal company offices and I consulted with the selective service people in Sydney, who have a pretty efficient set-up. Nobody can knock selective service as far as I am concerned; it has done a pretty good job. I said that I would like to know what proportion of service personnel coming back who had previously been employed in the coal mines were prepared to go back to the mines. The figures were startling. Of 1,000 men discharged from the service, 82 per cent refused to go back to mining coal. Was it because they were lazy? No. The fact of the matter is that when a man spends 
four or five years in the service he does not come back to civilian life the way he went in. These men are not physicaly fit to go back into that type of employment. The department did have established in that area during the war something that would have overcome this difficulty to some extent. There is now a large number of young people who have not been employed in the mines but who want to go into the mines, and if the apprenticeship system which was set up during the war under the war emergency production order had been continued, it would have helped to solve the problem to some extent. The young men on discharge from the service could go and see their rehabilitation officer if they wanted to go back into the coal mines, and if that school for training apprentices were still in operation these boys could be trained for work at the coal face. There is no employment on datal wrnrk for them because they are not qualified, but in the short time the school was in operation 95 per cent of those who applied for training were sent to work on the coal face. That system was discontinued five or six months ago; none of these schools is now operating. They were doing a first-class job and would have served a useful function in the rehabilitation set-up. Then you would not have in one spot alone 493 vacancies for qualified coal miners that cannot be filled.
The service personnel coming out are not physically fit to go back to coal mining. But you could have been training these ^young fellows during the past few months and that would have overcome the difficulty to some extent. On two occasions I questioned the minister in the house about these schools, because I thought that this apprenticeship set-up in the coal mines was one of the best things the department had done. It elevated coal mining to the status of a trade and gave the young fellows going into the mine an opportunity to learn the trade under proper instructions. The rates they were paid in these schools were very fair. In addition the boys were paying their way through the coal they produced, which offset the cost of operating the schools. The system was run on a fifty-fifty basis between the government and the coal company, but as I said, it has been allowed to peter out. When I questioned the minister on two occasions as to whether the schools would be carried forward into the post-war period he assured me that so long as he was Minister of Labour and had anything to do with the operation of that department the schools would be continued and the apprenticeship system as applied underground in the mines would be carried on. It was

Demobilization-Labour
serving a useful function in training young fellows in the trade of coal-mining, and it would be a step in the right direction, I submit, to reestablish this system.
There is another thought I would like to leave with the minister with respect to unemployment, and he might check on this with the Minister of Finance. I heard the Minister of Finance say in the house on .two occasions when discussing the excess profits tax that the tax was being rebated to corporations for the definite purpose of creating a backlog of funds that would be useful in creating new *employment in the reconversion period. All through the war this tax has been rebated to corporations to the extent of twenty per cent, and last year's budget raised the rebate to forty per cent. That is going to run into a lot of money. Here is a case in point. Canada Car and Foundry operated in Amherst, .Nova Scotia, and they made a considerable amount of money during the war period. They were allowed this rebate of twenty per cent of the excess profits tax-and what happened? Immediately after the war was over, the plant was closed. What happens to the excess profits tax rebated to a company that closes out its plant immediately on the cessation of hostilities? What happens to that twenty per cent, now forty per cent? They made that money in that plant.
But it was hot paid.

It will be paid, and I say that there is a large backlog of money. The Minister of Labour is responsible for employment, and I submit that he has the right to ask the Minister of Finance to see that that money is used specifically for the purpose of creating new employment in the post-war period in that district. The Minister of Labour has a right to say that that money should be spent in the community in which it was earned, rather than be given to that particular operator to help him create some new industry elsewhere. He might buy that plate mill which the Minister of Reconstruction is selling in Sydney and start) a government operation there, and I can assure him that we shall be able to find a market for all his plate. I leave this thought with the minister, because this question is tied up with the providing of employment. If we are going to pay back millions of dollars in these rebates, we should see to it that the money is used for the purpose for which it was intended.
I want to say a few words on unemployment insurance from the angle of employment. I am not satisfied with the machinery that has been provided by the department to determine new employment and the discontinuing of unemployment insurance payments.
I have a case in point, with all the evidence before me, but I shall not go into it at length. The minister knows that I have checked the case of Lillian Bateman of Sydney, Nova Scotia. The details briefly are these: Previous wages, $80 a month; five months unemployed; directed to several employers who refused to take her; directed to a large firm to do window-dressing at $12 a week, something for which she had no aptitude or training. The work was not comparable, the wage was not comparable, and she had no training in that work. The determining factor seems to be the length of time you are unemployed.
I do not think it should be.
The unemployment insurance commission in the first instance turned down this girl's claim. She appealed to the board of referees. The board of referees in my opinion was a very competent body. It had a broad-minded lawyer on it. The Dominion Steel and Coal company also had their representative on it, and we had D. W. Morrison, ex-president of district 26 of the mineworkers, who has held that position for twenty odd years. So I aim sure that the case would be thoroughly ironed out by the board. The board ruled that the young lady should get her unemployment insurance. The commission appealed that ruling. Then the case went to a one-man judge, Mr. Lueien Cannon. He heard the case in Ottawa on May 21, 1945. I have read over the whole case. I am not going to put it on the record, but I absolutely disagree with the judge's finding. Moreover I think that that set-up is bad. I do not think that one man should be given the right to throw overboard the decision of a competent three-man board. And mind you, they are right in the community where the problem affects the people. But when you pass the matter along to the city of Ottawa, where most people live in a vacuum, having little touch with the ordinary things of life, and have one man make the decision, you cannot expect to have the question settled. I have read Mr. Cannon's decision and his reasons for it, and I do not think there is anything in the memorandum setting out his decision that justifies him in that decision. He based it on one consideration and one only, namely, that she had1 been unemployed a reasonable time and should: take other employment at $12 a week, at window-dressing, which is a technical occupation for which one must have training. She had none.
The minister and the deputy minister I know are interested in these matters, are sympathetic and realistic about them, and I think they should decide that this umpire is
Demobilization-Labour

unnecessary. If the commission says, "This claim should be checked," and you pass it over to the three-man board, then the decision of that board in the community should stand; the matter should not be passed along to an umpire in Ottawa who has very little idea of what the problem is.
I do not believe in one-man decisions. I can be wrong so many times myself when I think over a question that I always like to talk things over with other people. It gives one a new slant.

That is just what judges do.
_ Mr. GILLIS: I wonder. At any rate, while judges have their place, I do not think it is on boards of this kind.
I have tried to !be helpful and in doing so I have merely .pointed out things that I believe are wrong. I do not think, judging from trends across Canada to-day, that we shall have very much peace in this country in the field of employment and in all related matters for the next couple of years. In my opinion we are going the wrong way about it. We are setting up unwieldy machinery, delegating the right, to private enterprise to go ahead and do the job. And they are not doing the job.
Last night I listened to the radio and heard the announcement that three more plants had closed down in Nova Scotia over night, without warning, one in the constituency represented by the Minister of Finance.. Crops are bad, the commentator stated. Things are in. a terrific state in Kentville. The plight is terrible, with three plants closed overnight. In short, that province to-day is faced with complete unemployment from one end to the other, and there seems to be no responsibility on the part of the people who have the job to do.
As soon as the war was over we should have recognized the importance of placing war workers and getting service personnel back into gainful employment. We should have recognized that this would take time and would .be difficult. These people should not have to bear all the suffering. One of the first things the Minister of Reconstruction should have done was to set up a labour-management committee, drawn from industry, which would sit in with him and plan matters, studying every question pertaining to industry. The minister may tell me that he has a committee of that kind, but I do not think so. I suggest that the personnel should come from the rank and file of the union members.
The organization of the garment workers should give us a lesson. They are working in [Mr. Gillis.I
cooperation with industry and the union planning reconversion, and there is no unemployment. The whole thing is running like clockwork, because industry and the organization are (working together.
The Minister of Reconstruction has a difficult job of reconversion, and he should have called in the ^union heads and sat down with them and tallied things over. They would have done the job with, less difficulty. In my opinion we should set up a minimum subsistence income for all service personnel coming back and finding it impossible to get work, and that income should be at least $25 a week. It should apply to the. war workers equally. They will be unemployed for some time. Instead of wasting words we should have established that income. It could have been done by augmenting the amount that is being paid by way of unemployment insurance, but instead of that :we have an army running around the country trying to find something that does not exist-work. And there will be none for some time. In the meantime, many war workers have taken on the obligation of homes. They have started buying houses and now they find themselves without any income.
There are many other matters that I might have discussed at length, but I think these two steps that I have mentioned in the field of employment are very important; first, getting the cooperation of people who understand the job at the bottom, talking it over with, the minister and working out a solution with the advice of people who come directly in contact with the workers in the plants; and second, establishing a minimum subsistence income. All we are doing now is giving relief for the time being, and the service personnel coming back are bitter when they think they have to go back to that kind of thing. As I said when I got up to speak, I did not intend to criticize.
I want to be helpful and to point out the difficulties as I see them. If matters are discussed in this way we have some hope of a solution. These things are not mysterious; the solution is a matter of plain common sense, What is lacking is the will to do something. That is the trouble. There is too much delayed action, too much waste of time. The Minister of Labour has a tough job, but let me say that no job is too tough if you face up to it.
I would like to see you tackle it.

That is exactly what I am saying. Take the Ford strike. I am not going to discuss that because it is the minister's problem, but he is still where he was when we first talked about it. I would have put

Demobilization-Labour
a controller in the plant within the first twenty-four hours after the Ford company showed me that they were unreasonable; and the minister is still faced with that. You cannot do anything else. There is no legislation in this province to which you can refer. Ford has slapped the whole government and eyeryone else [DOT] in the face. The union has backed up as far as it can go, and still the matter is where it was before. The struggle that kills most people is the fight within themselves. . I repeat, I would have put a controller in long ago, and the minister is still in the position where he will have to do that.
I would suggest to any members of this house who may have influence with the Ontario government that they advise the authorities there to call a session of the legislature and pass a trade union act for this province so that the same difficulty will not arise again. It is really a provincial matter until such time as we change the British North America Act and make it national. That is the only solution. If we keep on quibbling as we are doing, if we keep on guessing and trying to make things work, we shall find ourselves behind the eight ball within the next year or so. We must face up to the problem and run the country in the interests of all the' people instead of in the interests of any particular group. It would not worry me much to tell Ford what I thought, or to tell the union either, if I thought they were wrong.
I have already made my statement this afternoon on union security, and I have stated that the great majority of the people who discuss it do not understand it. The mechanics are simple. I know, because we fought it out when the going was tough and we had no parliament to appeal to, when the coal companies had private police forces and you could not meet in a hall but had to assemble in somebody's house. On any of these matters it is a question of being fair and square no matter whom you offend, so long as it is in the best interests of the people of this country.

It was my intention to wait
until the estimate in regard to the amount spent on the Japanese in this country was before the committee before I said anything; but since this debate was opened last night and certain speeches on the Japanese were made by hon. members on the other side of the house I feel compelled to say a few words now.
May I ask the hon. member to speak a little louder so that we may be able to hear what he is saying.

It is not very often that any hon. member or even anyone in the gallery has any difficulty in hearing what I have to say. Let me assure the hon. member that before I am through he will be able to hear what I have to say because there are things that I wish to say particularly to the members of his group.
Hurrah!

Do not wave the flag too soon
because the show is just beginning. First may I say this to the Minister of Labour. It is perfectly true that he wants to get his estimates through; it is perfectly true that the house wants to get -home before Christmas, but I wish to assure him that he will not have to read through my speech or wait very long to know what I really mean or for the committee to know what I mean. Generally speaking, I come to the point very quickly. I assure him and the committee that I shall not cover ground that has been already covered in this debate if I can avoid doing so.
First of all, may I deal with the statements that have been made outside this house against those of us from British Columbia who have taken the stand that the Japanese in our province and in other places should be sent out of Canada. While I do not intend to exhibit the heat that I think the hon. member for Vancouver East exhibited last night, I shall however exhibit heat against those who accuse me of raising this question and holding the views that I do simply on account of racial hatred. I deny that absolutely. It appears that if you differ with some people their main argument is that you are either a fascist or racially minded.
When I came to the house in 1931 I introduced a resolution, long before the Japanese question cropped up, to eliminate them from the Fraser river fishing. Before I get through with my remarks I shall ask any hon. member who feels like doing so to rise in his place and advocate that he is in favour of the Japanese going back to the fishing industry. May I tell the committee just why I introduced that resolution? At that time I discovered that Japan was in control of our fishing industry and that our own white Canadians were afraid of their lives to throw a net into the Fraser river opposite and below Steveston. I made up my mind then that I would do what I could to retrieve our heritage for our own people. I notice that a Doctor Sedgwick of British Columbia, a university
Demobilization-Labour

professor, had something drastic to say about those of us who hold the views I do. We have been called un-Christian and other names as well. Last evening the hon. member for Vancouver East and the leader of the C.C.F. party spoke about certain members holding views and referred to them as un-Christian. Well, I want to tell him and the other members of his party that when I want views on Christianity I will not go to any of that group to find out what Christianity really means, nor will I go to Doctor Sedgwick or Professor Angus or even some ministers of the gospel who are doing a great disservice to this country in making the^remarks they are making.
I hold the views I do rightly or wrongly. When we speak about hatreds in this country, to me the most dangerous hatreds are those that have, been built up since 1933, ever since the C.C.F. party came into being. That party has built up hatred of one class against another in this country. You can sense it everywhere at the present time. In almost every district in Canada where I have gone I have felt it; I have felt it in my own district, the hatred of one class of another. This is to my mind a bad thing to do. Members of that group get up and accuse us of raising racial hatreds. Others say that some of us should be put behind the bars. I know whom I would put behind the bars. There are some members of the legal profession, the ministerial profession and some professors whom I think it would be well for Canada to restrain in some way or other.

Fascism.
Mr. MaeINNIS: They did that in Germany.

I now wish to deal with the matter without any degree of rancour at all. I want to deal with it in a practical way, and put forth some arguments to the committee and the country which so far have not been answered. There has been a lot of sentimental slosh outside the house, and there has been a lot of sentiment placed on the record here which I shall try to expose or correct. At least I am going to put some practical questions and practical matters before the committee and the country, and I hope that some hon. member will get up and answer them if he can.
With regard to the statement made by Sedgwick and others that the Japanese were removed from British Columbia at the time of Pearl Harbor because of the hysteria which existed in British Columbia, may I correct that immediately and put it right? Is there a man in this house who will rise in his place at this time and say that he knew the
[DOT]'Mr. Reid.]
Japanese would never attack British Columbia? Just think back to the time of Pearl Harbor. Our defences were then next to nothing. No one knew where and when the Japanese navy or aircraft would attack. For safety reasons the government did a splendid thing at that time by immediately taking all the boats of the Japanese fishermen and removing the Japanese into camps or into the interior back from the coast.
May I make this statement. This year I happened to go up the coast, and the captain of the C.P.R. boat pointed out to me, so long as daylight lasted, that in all the long inlets all the way from Vancouver to Prince Rupert, at all strategic points on our coast, there were Japanese houses. Does any hon. member say that that was not by design, that it was just accidental that these Japanese houses were right at the head of bays looking up the long bay and out to the ocean? Will any man say that if the Japanese had been left on the coast of British Columbia and Japan had attacked us, the Japs would not have helped them? If he does I shall tell him that he had better go back to the people of British Columbia and tell them that story, and I have an idea what kind of answer he would receive because no one would believe him.
It is all very well to talk of their loyalty now. I am going to put this practical question to the committee. I realize it is very difficult to say who is loyal and who is not; but it is my view, sir, that they kept quiet under the hand of the higher-up Japanese. If the Canadian born are loyal Japanese, why is it that no mention has been made of Japanese atrocities or even the defeat of Japan in the Japanese paper published here, called the New Canadian? This paper is published by young men and women born in this country who have been educated in our schools and colleges, and who those foolish professors and unwise preachers contend are truly Canadians. I ask them this question. If they are truly Canadians, why have they been silent and were silent in their own paper for the entire month of August and the following months as well? Not a word was said about atfocities, no. Not even a word was said about the defeat of Japan. I can understand their not saying anything about atrocities. Probably they did not want to raise any hatreds. I can forgive them for that. But why, if they were Canadians, did they not publish anything in their paper about Japan being defeated? Strange they did not mention it. Not one voice was raised in their paper. I am particularly pointing my

Demobilization-Labour
finger at the C.C.F. group,, because they are the ones who say that the Japs are truly Canadians.

You are the ones who
brought them in.
You cannot lay that at my door.
We are the ones who moved them out.

May I now deal with the next point, namely, about their being loyal Canadians. I have asked this question of various groups; I have asked it from ministers and professors; I have asked it in this House of Commons, and I am going to ask it again, and shall be pleased if any hon. member following me will rise in his place and answer the question. Can a person who is born in this country be a truly Canadian citizen if he owes first allegiance to the country from which his father came? Every Japanese in this country was, before the war-and I believe they still are-duly registered with Japan; and as such they have been looked upon by that government as Japanese citizens. As a matter of fact, when Japan was counting the number of fishermen employed she always included in that number the number of Japanese fishermen in British Columbia. And when a Japanese died the undertaker had to send his birth certificate and death certificate to the government of Japan, even though the man -was born here.
I ask this further question: If they are Canadian citizens, then why has not one of them got up and publicly renounced the Emperor of Japan and the Japanese government?
