Why have they not stood up and said, "I am a Canadian; I was bom here of Japanese parents, but I am a Canadian. I have no allegiance to Japan. They do not have any hold on me at all."
But, no; a great silence from all the Japanese here. And I ask those people who are criticizing me and holding up the Canadian-born Japanese, to answer this question: Why has not one of those Japanese renounced his allegiance to Japan? My advice to the government is not to make one of them a Canadian citizen unless they did so.
We come now to the question of assimila-bility. I know that many others and I differ on this subject. Some of them say that they are assimilable and that intermarriage with the Japanese should be carried out. But I notice they are always the ones who want that kind of experiment tried out on someone else's family, not on their own. If I were in
a carping mood this afternoon I would certainly take grave exception to the statement made by a former C.C.F. member of the legislature who, thank heaven, was defeated in the last election but who said in Victoria that in her opinion the Scots were harder to assimilate in this country than the Japanese. I can assure you of this, sir, that if I had been present when it was said in the provincial house there would have been more said and done about it than was said or done. No greater insult has been lodged against any race than for a member to get up in the legislature of British Columbia and say that the Scottish people were harder to assimilate than the Japanese. The Japanese cannot be assimilated.
The Scots are the most generous people in the world.
These are the people who are saying that I am raising racial cries; yet they expect us to swallow these insults. I could say plenty about what has been said about myself, about being a foreigner.
You are.
Who said that?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If that statement were made it should be expunged from Hansard.
I thought I heard it; I hope I did not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am directing Hansard that if the statement were made it should not appear in Hansard.

On a point of order, I do not wish to take issue with your instructions to Hansard, Mr. Chairman, but I think you are going beyond your authority when you issue such instructions. That cannot be done without unanimous consent of the house.

As no one answered when I asked who said it, I do not suppose it is on Hansard, so that we do not have to worry about it. But if it is, I will take care of the matter. Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for the interruption.
I am placing these practical matters before those who hold views which are opposite to mine. I am not raising any racial cry, but I maintain to those people that the Japanese are a non-assimilable race, and that as such they are a danger for the present and1 future of Canada. Second, I have spoken against dual citizenship. At one and the same time they cannot be citizens of two countries.
I know that sometimes it has been asked: Why not criticize the Germans in this country? Why not criticize the Italians? Why pick
Demobilization-Labour

on the Japanese? There, again, I should' like to explain some of the reasons why I have taken issue with the Japanese. So far as I know, neither of the countries mentioned has laid claim to those born in. Canada, nor have I ever heard of a German or an Italian born in this country going back to do military duty in Germany or Italy.
I make the statement, without fear of successful contradiction, that the Japanese came to this country under a definite plan of the Japanese war lords. It is true that in the first instance they were brought here because they offered cheap labour, but later they were brought or sent to this country under that definite plan of their war lords, one which looked toward1 the day when Japan would strike for the supremacy of the Pacific.
Has my hon. friend any definite authoritative evidence on that point?

I have this authority: I have one of the Japanese year books which shows that the Japanese government lent millions of dollars to their citizens to settle on the Pacific coast. And I cannot see a government like that of Japan lending their nationals great sums of money just for the welfare of those Japanese who came here.
Can the hon. member quote from the Japanese year book to that effect?

Yes, I can quote from the Japanese year book; and if the hon. member will look up the records of this house he will find that I mentioned it on another occasion. I quoted the Japanese year book for 1934 in that speech, showing that in that year 52 million yen were sent back by the Japanese on the Pacific coast to Japan. That was returnable money, as shown by the Japanese records. Will my hon. friend suggest that they would put it in the year book if it were not true?
How much money did they really send; that is what I am talking about?
We do not send professors over there to find out the things we want to know.

The 52 million yen of which I have spoken were not by way of gifts, but rather in the paying back of loans for their establishment in Canada. It was not a straight gift at all. I am not speaking about gifts. I am speaking about a different matter entirely, about a business transaction carried out years ago by the Japanese government.
Let me come now to some statements which were made the other night by the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member
for Kootenay West. I have always differed with the hon. member for Vancouver East regarding the resolution he placed before the house in 1936. I make no bones about the matter; I voted against it. Why should I make any bones about it? I believe it was he and Mrs. Maclnnis that published a booklet and spread it widely throughout the Fraser Valley in which they mentioned particularly Tom Reid. I do not mind that. The publishing of the book has done me no harm, because I am still a member of the House of Commons.
It would be free advertising.

Yes, but of a doubtful kind. Be that as it may, I would ask hon. members who are interested in the matter to look at Hansard for February 20, 1936, the day the resolution was introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver East. Any hon. member who is interested will find that, although the resolution, as he read it to us last night, quoting from one of the little pamphlets that were circulated, states specifically:
Therefore be it resolved that, in the opinion of this house, the government should take the necessary measures to exclude from the country all persons belonging to those groups to whom we do not grant the full rights and privileges of citizenship . . .
-the fact remains that at least eighty-five or ninety per cent of his entire speech was devoted to the Japanese. Very little was said about other orientals included in the resolution-the Chinese, or those who come from India, and whom we describe as Hindus. The question of Indians was involved in that resolution and they are British subjects. The question of the Chinese was also involved. While they are orientals, they represent a diminishing problem in British Columbia. But if you look over that speech carefully and without bias you will come to the conclusion that the resolution was aimed1-this is my opinion at least.-against the Japanese. I have often wondered why the hon. member for Vancouver East, when he wras devoting his speech to the Japanese, did not mention the Japanese specifically in his resolution.
The resolution had another weakness. It asked that we. exclude from this country those races to whom we do not give the vote. Please note that would refer to one province only, because in all the other provinces Hindus, Japanese and Chinese can vote.
If the Japanese are worrying about losing the franchise it seems to me strange that they should be reluctant to stay in those provinces which grant them the franchise. But no; they

Demobilization-Labour
are all willing to come back to British Columbia-if we allow them to. If I know the people of British Columbia, and I think I know them just as well as any member from that province; I know that if you put that to a vote-I am willing that it should go to a vote-they will state in unmistakable terms that all be returned to Japan.
It was stated by the Minister of Labour last night that 10,000 or so may be returned and that the remainder will be spread throughout the other provinces. I am wondering under what act we shall be able to keep people from travelling from one province to another. I doubt if it can be done. I feel in my heart and mind that once the restrictions are lifted, every last Jap will go back to British Columbia.
I should like to offer some criticism of some of the provinces that criticize us. These provinces seem reluctant to keep the Japanese. They contend, however, that British Columbia should take them but they do not want them. This is now a national problem and the future of the country is involved. The only way to handle this unassimilable race is to send them back. As is well known, over
10,000	of the Japanese signified their willingness to return to Japan. The hon. member for Vancouver East has disputed the minister's statement, but he made it again most emphatically. I am glad the Minister of Labour did say that no duress or compulsion had been used. I would point out to the hon. member for Vancouver East and the rest of the committee that before any step was taken by the government, before the R.C.M.P. went around and asked them to sign that paper, a great number of Japanese, many Canadian born, wrote to the Spanish consulate of their own volition and asked that they be returned to Japan.
How many?

I cannot give the exact number and the hon. member will just have to take my word for it, but my information is that there were something like 2,200, most of them Canadian born, who requested the Spanish consul to have them returned to Japan. I realize that some of these Japanese may be loyal citizens, but when I visited the camp that was set up in Hastings park in Vancouver I found that there was a group there who had made it abundantly clear, when the Spanish consul visited the camp, that they were in this country at the request of Japan, and that they looked to Japan for protection. Of course they thought Japan was going to win, and they boldly said, "We will put it all over you; you will be working for us when Japan is the boss." These same
bold Japs in the camp at Hastings park were making it known that they did not care what happened, that we could do what we liked with them. Some of the same Japs later infiltrated into the various camps throughout the country.
I should like to refer to one or two of the statements made last night by the hon. member for Kootenay West. He referred to various meetings that had been held at which resolutions had been passed in favour of keeping the Japanese here. He mentioned the British Columbia municipalities. It is true that on two occasions when a resolution was brought up at their convention it was turned down, but there was a reason. I should like to remind the members of the Liberal party, of the Conservative party and of the Social Credit party that they could take a leaf out of the book of the C.C.F. party on political manipulation. They have seen to it that, wherever possible, members of their organization shall belong to municipal councils.
A great majority of the council members who attended those conventions were members of the C.C.F. and opposed any move to send the Japs back. They could not do otherwise because their leaders had spoken. At the first convention the resolution was lost, but in 1945 there was a different story. The hon. member for Kootenay West said that in the eastern part of British Columbia they had passed resolutions in favour of the Japs, but he did not tell the committee about the west. One of the largest conventions of municipalities was held at the coast in 1945, and they passed a resolution containing views similar to those which I and others hold.
With regard to the meeting at Richmond, to which he referred, which is in the riding that I have the honour to represent, he did not tell the committee the whole story. I had nothing at all to do with the first meeting called, but I was invited to attend. There were 450 fishermen at that meeting, and the hon. member made no mention of the fact that, with the exception of one man, who I understand was sent there to speak in their favour, the meeting was unanimously against the Japanese.
Then a small group of men who were endeavouring to have the Japanese repatriated attended a later meeting. The information I have is that that meeting was plugged by a group from the university, engineered to a great extent by this same Doctor Sedgewick. I was not at the meeting, but that is the information I have. The meetings were held at places only five miles apart. I thought it strange that at one meeting the members were unanimous for the repatriation of the

Demobilization-Labour
Japanese, and yet at another meeting, held two weeks later and only five miles away, a motion to repatriate them was lost. My further information is that a row developed, which I understand was engineered in an effort to mix up the meeting by somebody from the university who came for that very purpose. They did not belong to the municipality; they lived in Vancouver and other districts.
They are dangerous people.

Who, the university
people?

I think I have said all I need say without covering ground that I have covered before. Would there be anything wrong with giving the boys who fought and bled for this country an opportunity to say what they would do with the Japanese? Why are the people to whom I have referred afraid to leave the matter to our returned men? I have not projected into the argument this afternoon certain revolting stories, because one feels that he should not introduce particulars of atrocities, but I am just wondering how these foolish professors and unwise teachers really can believe in their own hearts that we have produced in this country a group of completely civilized human beings who are only one generation removed from savagery. If their attitude is right, that because these people have been born in British Columbia and raised in our schools, that makes them equal to our own citizens, we are perhaps wasting our time in sending missionaries to Japan. If their views are correct, why not bring more of the Japanese here to become civilized? I have often wondered if that thought has not percolated through the minds of those who hold this theory. But that is what they are saying, that all the Japanese who were born here are highly civilized, the equal of our own citizens. Yet one could mention, although I am not going to do so, case after case of Japanese who are at least accused of being the perpetrators of the very worst kind of crimes to our soldiers in Japan -men born and educated in the province of British Columbia. I leave that thought with this committee, and I want those who disagree with it to answer the questions I have raised: the question of dual citizenship, the question of assimilability; and to give the reasons they have, if any, why the Japanese paper published by Canadian-born Japanese has kept absolutely silent both on the atrocities of Japan and likewise on the defeat of Japan. It is very noticeable that this seeming change of tMr. Reid.]
heart by the Japanese who now want to remain here, has all taken place since Japan was defeated.

Mr. Chairman, there are
many new members in this House of Commons, and during the discussions this session I have noticed that they have given very careful consideration to serious issues that were brought before them. This afternoon I should like them to follow me in my discussion of the Japanese question, because it has now ceased to be the. problem simply of those Canadians who face the Pacific and has become the problem of all Canada. I shall discuss it from that point of view.
Before doing so, I Should like to say a word about my good friends the hon. member for Vancouver East, a member of the C.C.F. party, and the hon. member for Kootenay West, an ex-member of the C.C.F. party but who apparently is still thoroughly in accord with the C.C.F. on their Japanese policy. On this question as on many others they fail completely to face the facts. It reminds me of their attitude when Canada went to war. Here we were entering a life-andkieath struggle, and yet that party took the stand that Canada must not send one man from her shores; it would be all right to send munitions or to send food, but we must not send one man. They were totally wrong then. They failed at that time to face the facts, but it was just what one might have expected from them because in the years preceding the war they had done everything they could to break down the defence forces of Canada and had advocated a one-sided disarmament. Their heads completely in the air, their feet right off the ground, they failed to face the problems that had to be settled by the Canadian people.
That has been their attitude. And last night they presumed to say that on this Japanese question they represent Christianity. Well, that is a tall order. I sometimes think they take themselves far too seriously. Certainly they have no corner on representing Christianity, any more than they have a corner on representing the common man-another title they claim so often. But I am sure of one thing, that on this Japanese question they do not represent the people of British Columbia. Their overwhelming defeat in the provincial election in British Columbia a few weeks ago showed that, when they had ten of their sitting members defeated, lost ten of their leading men, and yet their provincial candidates did not go nearly as far on this issue as the hon. member for Vancouver East; they rather hide their heads when he takes his stand on this question.

Demobilization-Labour
The present Japanese situation is the result of the failure of the Canadian people to heed those Canadians who live west of the Rocky mountains. They failed to heed them right down through the years, for half a, century. This issue first arose nearly fifty years ago. When the Japanese started to come to Canada our predecessors in this house protested against their admission session after session. The dominion government failed to do an}' thing about the matter. The imperial government recommended to Ottawa that Canada should pass a Natal act similar to the act passed by Australia and South Africa, under which there is a Language test which has had the effect of keeping the Japanese out of those two dominions. The British Columbia legislature passed a Natal act six times, and six times it was disallowed by the dominion government, in several cases at the instigation of the Japanese consul general in Vancouver, who complained bitterly each time British Columbia passed such an act. There were riots in Vancouver about 1907 or 1908 over this Japanese, question because the Japanese-were being allowed to come in by the thousand. As a result of the riots, a gentleman's agreement was entered into and the number of Japanese coming in was reduced; it was reduced again in the twenties, but there were Japanese coming into Canada right up to the time that Japan struck on December 7, 1941.
Practically all of them settled on the coast of British Columbia. The Minister of Labour gave the figures last night. About 95 per cent remained in British Columbia, and remained right in the coastal area. We had twice as many Japanese in proportion to our population in British Columbia as the state of California and three times as many as the state of Washington, which adjoins us on the south. There these people were, settled on the British Columbia coast, in contact with Japan all the time, with Japanese merchant vessels coming into our harbours, with fishing boats coming over, and with in many cases, the Japanese in British Columbia sending their children back to be educated in Japan. There were 1,500 children of Japanese in British Columbia in Japan at the time of Pearl Harbor. Those young Japanese in many cases went back and took military training and in due course came back to British Columbia. The city of Vancouver was the centre of Japanese activity in Canada. It was not here in Ottawa where the ambassador resided, but in Vancouver where the consul general had his office.
In 1940 the Japanese government took a census of the Japanese in Canada, and I have here a newspaper clipping of that time in which the census is explained in these words: It is the regular ten-year census taken of Japanese at home and abroad.
Births in Canada were registered with the Japanese consul in Vancouver so that they might not lose their status as Japanese subjects; help was given through the consul's office so that' the Japanese might buy up farms and engage in fishing and other industries; and, the most serious aspect of all, Japanese are emperor-worshippers; the emperor is their god. Hon. members have seen how this summer the Japanese emperor had merely to say the word that the war was over and Japanese armies stopped fighting in every theatre, showing the total power of the Japanese emperor over these people. How can one expect the vast majority of them to be loyal Canadians first? I have no doubt there are some, but how can one expect the vast majority, the rank and file of the Japanese in Canada, to have loyalty to Canada first and to Japan second?
Something has been said of naturalization. It is an accepted fact that the great majority of the Japanese who became naturalized did so in order to get fishing licences. They could not fish without becoming British subjects. A commission inquired into this question as far back as 1900. I am not going to quote their finding; I did that two years ago, but any hon. members who are interested can find it in the sessional papers of this house for 1902.
The hon. member for New Westminster has pointed out that they were located at strategic points on our coast. They had 1,100 fishing boats. They knew the coast far better than our own people did. There was spying. We hear the statement made at different times that nothing which was at all improper was done by these people. Just six days ago dispatches appeared in the press across Canada; I have one here from the Vancouver Sun:
Jap spies busy here during war.
Japanese spies in Vancouver were_ instructed to attempt to secure information during the war on such matters as ship movements, military mobilization and geographical facts, according to a report to-day from Washington, D.C.
These disclosures were made when exhibits were placed before the congressional committee investigating the happenings which plunged the United States into war and temporarily broke the backbone of the American fleet at Pearl Harbor.
Copies of a message seeking such information were forwarded to Jap agents in Vancouver and Ottawa, it was stated, but its source was not identified . . .
Demobilization-Labour

This spy activity began months before Pearl Harbor.
One need not be surprised1 at that finding, because they were spying everywhere that the Japanese landed. I do not suppose anyone will question that fact. I have here, for example, a press dispatch of February 24, 1942, from London, headed:
Tremendous extent of Jap espionage becoming apparent.
It points out:
Japanese espionage has encircled the world. The latest disclosure of its efficiency comes from Darwin, Australia, where the accuracy of the recent bombing by the yellow air raiders has been such that knowledge of every important target must have been gained by the enemy.
Remember, for many years Australia has not allowed Japanese to enter, and had only about 2,500 when the war broke out.
Also, among Dutch people in London, it is well known that for years past Japanese fishermen throughout the whole Netherlands East Indies collected military information on a wholesale scale.
That is the background. These are some of the happenings which so worried the people of British Columbia. On December 7, 1941, Japan struck at Pearl Harbor. In the previous year, on September 27, 1940, she announced her alliance with Germany and Italy. I very well remember, the night after Japan struck at Pearl Harbor, we were warned that Vancouver was to be attacked. We had our first black-out. Then we heard over the radio the order that all Japanese fishing boats must report at certain centres. The boats were called in right away. That was a very wise move on the part of the government. But after that was done nothing else happened. The Japanese were allowed to remain sitting in these different locations. I myself was taken by the commander of the Vancouver defence area some weeks later to see the gun position defending the mouth of the Fraser river. Between the huts in which the men lived and the guns was the home of the leading Japanese in that particular centre, and the army men were worried about the situation. Another friend of mine commanded a post out on the west coast of Vancouver island. He served with me in the last war. He said, "I have not my guns set up to protect against invasion; I have them trained on the Japanese village; that is where my trouble will come from if it comes." At that time we had on the Pacific coast fewer aeroplanes than could be carried on one Japanese aircraft carrier, and all but a handful of them were obsolescent. We had a divided command-a commander of the army, a commander of the navy, a commander of the air force-just as the Americans

had at Pearl Harbour when the Japanese struck there. Our position from a defence point of view was hopeless if the Japanese had cared to strike.
I have here a dispatch from Elmore Philpott, one of the leading columnists of Canada. He happens to be a very liberal-minded commentator: he was largely or partly responsible for the election of the hon. member for Kootenay West; he went there and helped him in his campaign; he also advocated the election of many members of the C.C.F.; and he advocated my own election. He lives in my riding; so that was what counted.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Pretty broadminded!

I have here an article of his which appeared some time in February, 1942. He says:
I do not know one responsible B.C. official, cabinet minister, police, forester or otherwise, who is satisfied with things as they are on the Pacific coast. Unfortunately the service men can't speak out.
Nobody needs to be a secret service agent to know that a Japanese fifth column will work wherever the Japanese government wants it to work. It is not a question of the loyalty or disloyalty of individual Japanese, native born or otherwise. In a total population of some
25,000	there is no conceivable way of keeping the Japanese government from planting or employing active fifth columnists to do whatever it wants done.
The entire Japanese population should be moved from this coast as soon as it is humanly possible. That means now-before an actual military action can take place.
As it is the government has only begun to deprive them of their radios, short wave or otherwise, on which they can take daily code messages. The government has not only allowed them to stay right beside guns-but it has left them close to vital power plants which are so poorly protected that they could be destroyed far more easily than the Normandie was fired last week.
There was grave danger of an attack on Canada's Pacific shores. That was the time when sabotage would have taken place. Had troops attempted to land they would have expected support from the local residents. A dispatch appeared in February'-, 1942, from the United States to this effect:
That's when the campaign of sabotage is to be waged. The reason there has been no outbreak of sabotage in the United States so far is that the Japanese government has ordered the Japs in this country to withhold such activities until the military attacks.
If the Japanese fleet had not been defeated at Midway, if the Japanese task force had not been turned back on its way to take Dutch Harbor in Alaska, there would probably have been a landing on the shores of British Columbia. I emphasize these things, since the cry is now raised that these Japanese were removed only because there was a lot of race

Demobilization-Labour
prejudice on the coast; there was a lot of racial hatred, and so the government moved them out. The demand for the removal of the Japanese came from the commanders of the forces and from public men. I have here a wire I received dated February 24, 1942, sent to me at Ottawa, signed by twenty-one or twenty-two of our leading citizens, among them Harold E. Winch, M.L.A., leader of the C.C.F. in British Columbia and Grant MacNeil, M1.A,, one of their outstanding figures, a man who served ably in this house from 1935 to 1940. The telegram says:
Owing to widespread public alarm over enemy aliens on the Pacific coast and especially respecting those astride vital defence points and with a view to stabilizing public opinion and in the interest of public safety the undersigned met and now urge:
1.	That military authorities be immediately authorized to remove enemy aliens from any and all points considered by military authorities essential in the interests of proper and adequate defence and public safety.
2.	That the evacuation of all those of Japanese origin from the Pacific coast area be proceeded with immediately and plans to this effect announced.
That wire does not show race prejudice but it does show deadly peril. A protected zone was set up extending 100 miles from the coast and including Vancouver island, the Queen Charlotte islands and other islands. In due course the government set up what was known as the British Columbia security commission, and an advisory committee to that commission was appointed. One member of the advisory committee was Mr. Winch, leader of the C.C.F., and the secretary of the advisory committee was Mr. Grant MacNeil. The Japanese were moved away from the protected area and settled in the interior of British Columbia. A few were sent east of the Rockies. But the provinces-and this is where the other provinces come into the picture-insisted, in the agreements which were made with the British Columbia security commission concerning these Japanese, that after the war the Japanese must be removed on the request of the particular province. I have here the agreement with Alberta dated May 6, 1942, of which paragraph 10 reads:
The commission agrees to remove or to have removed from the province, upon the termination of the state of war now existing between Canada and Japan, the Japanese temporarily placed or maintained within the province pursuant to the terms of this agreement as requested so to do by the province.
There was a similar agreement with Ontario and a letter containing the same understanding with Manitoba. I believe there was either a letter to or an agreement with the province
of Quebec-the minister can correct me there if I am wrong-and also, if you please, with the province of Saskatchewan.

There was nothing with
Quebec.

Some of the Japanese from the coast were interned. At one time over six hundred were in an internment camp in Ontario, and on October 31 of this year there were still interned in Ontario 416, of whom there were 168 Japanese nationals, forty-two naturalized Canadians, 203 born in Canada and three United States citizens. That number were still in internment camps. As time went on, the government decided on a dispersal policy. They did not say very much about it and I do not think they have been as frank with the Canadian people on this question as they might have been.
I think my hon. friend will admit that we have done a good job.
They have not said very much about it. They have not explained the position and they did not persuade the provinces to withdraw this provision.
I think we have done a good job notwithstanding some people in the last parliament.
I suggest that the government could have done a better job and I will show some ways in which they could have done so. May I call it -six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Before the committee rises, I wonder if I might appeal to hon. members to finish to-night. Are there many questions which hon. gentlemen wish to ask the Minister of .Reconstruction later in regard to his estimates? I am most anxious that we should finish the whole measure to-night so that we may go on to-morrow with the emergency powers 'bill, which is vital to the progress of the session.
The minister seems to be looking in my direction. I shall not detain the Minister of Reconstruction long this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Thank you.

When the Minister of Reconstruction was speaking to his estimates he volunteered to give a good deal of information that he was not prepared to give at the time. It would look as though this might be the only opportunity available.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We shall endeavour to finish with the Minister of Labour after eight o'clock and then have the Minister of Recon-
Demobilization-Labour

struetion answer such questions as are put to him. I trust that we shall have the resolution passed, reserving all rights to hon. gentlemen to ask questions under civil estimates which have not yet been dealt with.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose for the dinner recess I was outlining the moves which were taken to get the Japanese away from the protected area on the Pacific coast. The great majority were sent into the interior of British Columbia, but a small percentage were sent east of the Rockies where, in almost every case, they were under an agreement with the particular province in which they were settled that at the end of the war they would be returned to British Columbia upon request by that province. As the months went by the government tried to cariy out a policy of dispersal by persuading those Japanese to move east of the Rockies, and the younger aqd better ones west. Many of them have settled in eastern Canada on a permanent basis, and they deserve credit for having done so. Those who remained in British Columbia have been very hard to persuade to move. They have been very little interested in settling east of the Rockies. I think their whole plan is either to go back to Japan or to settle once more on the Pacific coast.
One feature which has not been emphasized during the debate is the attitude of many of the eastern centres. For example, take the city of Ottawa. This city has refused to allow any Japanese to settle, and yet the two Ottawa papers have been quite free in expressing their opinions editorially as to what British Columbia should do about the Japanese.
I hold in my hand the New Canadian, which is the publication of the Japanese. In the issue of November 25, 1944, we find the headline, "Canadian citizens refused trade licences in Toronto." Then in the- issue of September 2, 1944, we find this: "No Evacuees, says Chatham." There are many other cities in Canada which have refused to take any step to help solve the problem. Therefore we come to this position as of October 31 of this year; there were in British Columbia at that date 14,824; almost two-thirds of the Japanese in Canada are still in British Columbia; Alberta, 3,703.
Would my hon. friend like the latest figures? They are slightly different.

I would rather finish my remarks on this basis. These are the figures I got from the minister's department as of October 31. Saskatchewan has 160. Of those 160, only seventy-one have been evacuees. The others were there before the war. Manitoba has 1,171; Ontario, 3,509, which includes 416 who are interned; Quebec, 671, Nova Scotia one, and he was there before the war; New Brunswick ten, the Yukon and Northwest Territories twenty-nine, Prince Edward Island, none, a total of 24,078.
Bast summer the Prime Minister announced the policy of the government. In brief, it was to return to Japan those who wished -to go; to set up a loyalty commission to decide upon the loyalty or disloyalty of those who had not expressed a wish to go back; to send back those found disloyal; to disperse the rest across Canada, and that there would be no further immigration. . Eventually a survey began early in this year, 1945, of those who wished to go back to Japan. The people of Japanese origin across Canada were asked to make a choice. If they asked for repatriation, in each case they renounced their status as British subjects.
I hold in my hand another issue of the New Canadian, which gives the form they sign. It reads as follows:
1,	hereby declare my desire to
relinquish my British nationality and to assume the status of a national of Japan. Further, I request the government of Canada under the conditions set out in the statement of the Minister of Labour, dated February 13, 1945, to arrange for and effect my repatriation to Japan, together with my dependents under sixteen years of age as listed hereunder.
Where the Japanese was a Japanese national, he did not, of course, request the relinquishment of his status as a British subject. While this survey was being taken, the New Canadian kept advising those Japanese not to sign; it pleaded with them not to sign it, so that there is not much doubt about their knowing what they were doing. A large number did sign. I have here the figures as of August 31. They are a little different from those given last night by the minister; but they show by provinces; British Columbia, 8,941, and if every one of those went it would still leave British Columbia with 6,000 Japanese; Alberta, 571; that would leave about 3,100 in Alberta; Saskatchewan, two; Manitoba, 405, which would leave Manitoba with about 750; Ontario, 325, which would leave Ontario with 3,200; the mari-

Demobilization-Labour
times, none; the Yukon and Northwest Territories, none; internees, 216 of the 416 asked to be sent back to Japan; a total of 10,478. The minister gave a total of 10,347 last night.
After the survey had been completed, those Japanese who wished to be repatriated were moved into repatriation centres so that they could be sent back to Japan without further difficulty. I understand that since V-J day some have been trying to change their decision, and they are being stirred up constantly not only by the New Canadian, but also by pressure groups which have been formed in various parts of Canada. I think these pressure groups have little idea of helping to solve the problem. They do not seem to be worrying very much about the final solution of this problem. I suggest to the committee that what they are trying to do is to show how very broadminded they are at the expense of the people of British Columbia. That is pretty cheap business on an issue of this kind.
As yet no loyalty commission has been set up as promised by the Prime Minister, although the Department of Labour, through their British Columbia security commission, have extensive records of all those Japanese. Mark you, I think some of the most dangerous and some of the ones who are least Canadian are just cute enough to decline to sign the form to go back to Japan. They are waiting until the smoke blows away, and they plan to go on as they were doing before the war. For example, we have 200 internees who were sufficiently dangerous or obstreperous to be confined for several years. They have not asked to go back and presumably they are planning to stay here.
Then, I believe that all the Japanese nationals, as distinguished from naturalized Japanese, or those born in Canada, were not asked to sign one way or the other. ^ am told that by some of the officials of the British Columbia security commission. There was no requirement that all Japanese nationals should sign, and I believe quite a large number of them did not elect.
They were all invited to sign, if I might put it in that way.

They may have been invited to, but they were not required to. We should know what .the government intends to do with those nationals who have not signed one way or the other.
The greatest omission in the minister's statement last night was that he said nothing /whatsoever about the Japanese who are in the
other provinces, under an agreement to be taken away upon request at the end of the war. The attitude of these provinces is most significant. I have here another issue of the New Canadian, dated February 3, 1945, in which the hon. Mr. Fallow, acting premier of Alberta, is quoted as having said this:
When the war is over, these birds will have to get out.
He was referring then to Alberta. Then, the premier of Quebec, on March 16, is reported in this fashion:
Premier Duplessis told British United Press in Quebec city the provincial government would take constitutional means to prevent the establishment of Japanese there.
The premier of Ontario is quoted as follows on March 19:
It was not our choice these people should come into this province. As we understood, it was entirely a safety measure to move these people from British Columbia when it was thought there was possibility of invasion by Japanese forces. There is no reason an emergency measure of this kind should be employed to settle in this province Japanese whom we never sought and whom we would not have welcomed at that time.
I would ask at this time to hear from hon. members from those provinces as to what they think about this matter. What are they saying should be done with the Japanese in their provinces? Are they to be allowed to stay there, or are they to be put out? New Brunswick has only ten; yet the authorities at once gave an assurance to the, people of that province that the Japanese were there only during war time, and that they would go out when the war ended.
If they are to be allowed to remain in the other provinces, they must have the right to buy land and the right to go into business. They have not any of those rights at the present time, nor have they had since they were moved out of British Columbia.
So, you see, the problem is not yet being faced. This gives grave concern to the people of British Columbia, where we still have 14,824 Japanese. In addition, we may have all those sent back that the other provinces do not want. Then, after that, we might get those who will come back of their own free will, and who prefer to live in British Columbia. This means that the problem will be back exactly where it was before the war. That, I suggest to members of the house from other provinces, is unfair to the .people of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Hear, hear.

And we do not intend to be put in that position.
Demobilization-Labour

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Hear, hear.

We do not intend) again to see the Japanese gain, a foothold on the Pacific coast shoreline of Canada.
I suggest that some attention should be paid to what is said by those lads who have returned from Hong Kong. I have here a dispatch which puts on record the attitude of ten of those men who returned on October 4. They said:
"Don't let any Japanese settle in Canada. Their mental processes are different from ours and they will never adjust to the occidental way of life."
That's the unanimous indictment of the ten Canadian repats from Manila who arrived here yesterday on the United States transport General Lonyfitt."
I suggest these steps to the minister: First, the protected zone in British Columbia should be extended from the point 100 miles from the coast, right to the eastern boundary of the province. This should be maintained into the peace-time period, at least for a sufficient number of years to enable what Japanese remain in Canada to be properly settled elsewhere.
That was the policy of the Progressive Conservative party during the election, and for years prior thereto. The hon. member for Kootenay West said that we had no policy. Well, I think he was so busy quarreling with his C.C.F. friends that he did not have time to check up on a good many policies.
Do not worry; before the next election you and the Liberals will have the same policy.

In the second place I suggest that the government should send back those who have so requested. The minister spoke last night as though he might be allowing a whole Jot who were not Japanese nationals to change their minds. There may be some cases where injustices have been done, and those people should be given a further chance. But the vast majority knew what they were doing when they signed for repatriation, and the government should not be weak enough now to allow them to make any change.
Those who are found disloyal by the commission which is to 'be set up should be sent back. I think there is agreement on that point, on all sides of the house. However, that will still leave those who are not acceptable to the other provinces. And, by the way, this policy of making the whole of British Columbia a protected zone is the policy not only of the Progressive Conservative party but also of the Minister of Veterans

Affairs. A meeting on June 6, 1944, of the dominion convention of the Canadian Legion is reported as follows:
If the Japanese come back to British Columbia after the war, Hon. Ian Mackenzie will quit politics. That is by his own word.
Then, he said this at the time he was nominated-and I give him credit, because I think he meant it; a report of September 19, 1944, when he was nominated, credits him with this statement:
Not a single Japanese from the Rockies to the sea. I ask my fellow citizens of Vancouver Centre, and of British Columbia as a whole, to range themselves beside me on this issue and to serve notice on the rest of Canada that we will not have Japanese in this fair province.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Then, as I have said, there would still be those who are not acceptable in other provinces. I suggest to the minister that consideration be given to making the request that, in the peace treaty with Japan, arrangements be made for resettling these Japanese in the Pacific, with adequate financial compensation and, if necessary, under united nations trusteeship. There will have to be many shifts in population provided for in the peace treaties. I believe that already the Chinese are sending all the Japanese out of China, and that the British have done the same in Singapore. Population shifts will have to be made in many parts of the world, and I suggest that this is a proposal which should be given serious consideration by the government.
For fifty years, half a century, the voice of British Columbia has not been listened to on this question, although British Columbians were the Canadians directly affected. And now, from this new parliament, I ask that we be given a final solution of the problem.

I can think of no more urgent problem which could be discussed1 in this chamber than that of the estimates of the Department of Labour; and when I refer to an urgent problem I am not referring to the Japanese issue, which has received such lengthy debate. It is unfortunate, in fact, that the matter of the Japanese who reside in Canada comes under the Department of Labour, because surely there is sufficient to discuss in the field of labour-management relations in Canada, and especially at this time when we are in a state of reconversion from war to peace.
During the years of war all members of this house and all Canadians recognized that labour did a very fine job. Men and women worked on day shifts and night shifts; women and young girls left the small towns, the villages

Demobilization-Labour
and the farms to take up work which was quite hard for them to do. Men changed from town to town, from one job to another, and worked hard to produce the materials necessary for victor}*. Speaking last night, the minister paid a tribute to the workers who produced the weapons of war. He said:
I would be remiss if I did not say how splendidly our men and women played their part during the war years.
These are fine words, but the fact is that these people whose efforts were being praised, and they deserved to be, are to-day being confronted with many difficult problems. These workers through their unions adhered during war time to a "no strike" policy, but to-day in many industries they are being provoked into strikes. During the war many workers often felt that they had no other resort than to strike, and then their labour leaders would try to urge them to stay on the job despite all provocation. I saw a couple of union leaders who had received1 black eyes because they had urged the workers in a shipyard in Montreal to go back to work. It was not easy for trade union leaders, to convince the workers that they had to stand for all kinds of dirt because the weapons of war had to be produced.
As a reward, labpur to-day is being faced by a certain attitude on the part of some employers and, unless the government steps in, we shall have difficult times and instability for a long time to come. During war time I attended quite a number of union meetings in Quebec; I spoke to many workmen, and I have always been proud of the fact that it was lodge No. 712 of the Montreal aircraft workers, which contained a majority of French Canadian workers, that brought forth the idea of labour-management committees to increase production. They, too, are confronted to-day with difficulties.
There are some employers who unwillingly accepted collective bargaining in war time because there had to be production, but before the war was over they were planning to go back to what had obtained during pre-war years. The most outstanding example of this is the anti-union Ford Motor company. After seventeen months of boards and more boards, the workers had no' alternative than to strike. There comes a time when workers ask: What do we do next? Then comes the strike. The workers at Ford went out on strike and this strike has become a test for post-war labour-employer relations. It is also a test, as far as I am concerned, of the government's attitude toward rewarding workers who did such 47696-153
a fine job during war time. I must say that the government's role has not been the best; it has not been encouraging to labour.
On a number of occasions in this house we have heard the minister give the reasons for the delay in settling this strike. The company offered the alibi that the powerhouse was closed and that their executive staff could not get into the offices. We were told of the calamities that would befall the city of Windsor and the Ford Motor company if the power-house were not opened. That was the reason given for sending the police to Windsor. The R.C.M.P. went there; the provincials went there. The Ford Motor company does not seem anxious to open the power-house.
Acting in what I thought was a most conciliatory manner, the union offered to reopen the power-house and give the executive staff access to the offices. Negotiations were opened between the union and the company and every one hoped that an agreement would be reached. The minister spent a few' days there in a sincere effort to bring the two parties together, but sincerity does not always get results especially when one is confronted with an anti-union element that is ready to do everything in its power to smash thp union.
In a statement issued yesterday the company now charges that the union's offer to open the power-house was a hollow offer. On the other hand, the union states that when they got together with the company a few days ago for a discussion there was a basic understanding that the company would discuss the twenty-two points in dispute. But here is what happened, according to the union's statement:
We were amazed to discover at to-day's session, however, that the company was only prepared to discuss six minor points of the twenty-two in dispute. *
And again:
On the union security issue the company definitely refused to discuss any phase of the issue, even in exploratory fashion. When asked if it would discuss a mild form of union security as a tentative settlement pending further negotiations in order to bring about the resumption of the .plant in the interests of the workers and the nation, they gave a definite no.
A number of other suggestions were offered in the form of compromises but the company indicated in no uncertain manner that they were not willing to discuss any but the six points. They displayed a complete irresponsibility to the needs of the hour by refusing to discuss such vital issues as veterans' seniority, seniority, severance pay, hospitalization, insurance and reconversion committee, which are basic requisites to bargaining in good faith.
There are other employers, some anti-union, who are to-day watching the Ford Motor

Demobilization-Labour

company. If Ford is successful, then they feel they can start to try to smash the unions themselves. They are watching that giant of .ndustry; they want the day to come when they will have a free hand. We have an example of this in Toronto where at present there is a strike at Imperial Optical. This is a smaller company, but it is rather rich having had plenty of protection through special tariff arrangements and1 what-not.- This company refuses to deal with the union, despite the fact that over a year ago the union was certified as the bargaining agent. This company, and many others, are waiting to see what will be the outcome at Ford.
Where do we go from here? What now? I would say that these strikes show that there is something radically wrong with our. labour legislation. After all, the proof of the pudding is in the eating. If our labour legislation were better, we would not have so many strikes; we could look forward to a more peaceful future for labour and1 management. It is because our labour legislation is inadequate that we have these troubles to-day, and it is time that the government acted, especially in the Ford strike. That strike has now lasted for two months, affecting 10,000 workers in the Ford plant, 8,000 workers - in other plants, besides the many others who have been thrown out of work through the closing of the Ford plant. All these porkers want a settlement of the strike. What is necessary is that the government act. That is the only solution because the company will not yield. That is very clear from the full page advertisement that appears in to-day's papers, and I suppose it appears in all the newspapers throughout the country. They are paying for newspaper advertisements with deductions from taxes, to tell the country why they will not settle the strike. The government must act to-day. A few weeks ago the government appointed controllers for the packing plants, and the order in council stated that this action was taken because the people of Europe needed food and relief. What about the people in Windsor, the thousands of families who will starve unless this strike is settled soon? A controller is the only answer, and action must come soon. The strike should not have been allowed to drag along for so long.	.
The Minister of Labour in his report to the house last night, speaking of the problems confronting the country in connection with reconversion, said:
I am convinced of this, that just as we built the greatest industrial machine in the life of this nation, and built it in a very short time after the outbreak of war and the fall of France, given the cooperation of the Canadian people, leadership on the part of employers' iMr. Rose.]
and workmen's organizations and also in agriculture, together with this government, we can make just as big a contribution to peace as we made to the recent war.
I fully agree with that statement, but the situation is somewhat different now. In war time, when the government felt that it was necessary to control a certain mine because it contained precious metals, the mine was taken over. If a certain industry was not producing as rapidly as it should, the government stepped in and set up a crown company. If the management in a certain industry was not satisfactory, the government stepped in and changed the management. There was quite a bit of necessary intervention-some might call it interference-by the government to ensure that things ran smoothly. Are the government willing to do the same thing today? If they are, we should have no trouble in this country. If they are not; if they are to revert to a laissez-faire attitude, leaving the vast mass of people dependent for their livelihood upon a few individuals, we are bound to have trouble. It is the government's responsibility to guarantee that we have stable conditions and not to leave it to individuals. It is the government's responsibility to help avoid strikes by guaranteeing Canadians good wages and a full measure of security, because we all recognize, and those who do not should, that this period is a carryover of the war emergency; it is just as much an emergency as the war itself.
My party, the Labour-Progressive party, has a minimum programme which we believe the country needs at this time if we are to proceed smoothly and ensure that the people ' get more purchasing power and a greater security. Our minimum programme is this: (1) The universal application of the forty-hour week and an increase in wages to safeguard the take-home pay; (2) the amendment of P.C. 9384, the wage control order, to permit the raising of wage rates which are too low to provide for the minimum standard of health and decency; (3) the introduction of a national minimum wage rate of 55 cents an hour; (4) the amendment of P.C. 1003, the collective bargaining regulations, to provide for union security; (5) an increase of 50 per cent in unemployment insurance payments.
That is a constructive programme which should be implemented. These are things that need discussion at the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction. We know that this conference is not going to sail smoothly. The Montreal Gazette in this morning's issue reported that Premier Drew and Premier Duplessis had met at the Ritz-Carlton hotel in Montreal. That does not augur well for

Demobilization-Labour
the success of the conference. But whatever views may be expressed at the conference, an enlightened public opinion can force the delegates to change their minds. There are certain matters which have not been taken up by the conference which should be raised, and I have in mind particularly the problem of labour relations. In the proposals submitted by the government of Canada to the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction I find this with regard to wage control and collective bargaining:
Much has been said at various times about the desirability of uniformity throughout Canada of minimum wage standards, occupational coverage, maximum hours of work and minimum age of employment, consistent with justifiable local or regional variations in cost of living standards. The dominion government is most willing to discuss any proposals which might be made in these fields.
I regret that it was put as mildly as that. It was up to the government, just as it came along with proposals regarding health and old age pensions, to come along also with proposals respecting a minimum wage and a national labour code. There is a growing sentiment throughout the country in favour of a national labour code. It was interesting to note that in the province of Quebec, which is often referred to as an isolationist province, a labour delegation a few weeks ago proposed to Premier Duplessis a national code for labour.
I did not hear that. Did the hon. member say that the premier of Quebec wanted a national code?
No. A delegation representing the C.C.L. unions in the province of Quebec met the premier of the province and proposed a national labour code.
Does the hon. member think that is popular in Quebec?
This delegation, speaking on behalf of organized labour, made that proposal to the premier.
The hon. member does not really mean that?

I sincerely do. It was the opinion of the delegation representing the members of the C.C.L. unions in the province of Quebec. I was not there myself.
I know that all sorts of arguments are generally dragged out in opposition to a national labour code. The constitutional problem is raised. I say that if it is necessary to make changes in our constitution, those changes should be made.
47696-153*
In this atomic age we cannot live in the horse-and-buggy days of 1867. The bogey will be raised in connection with high wages that if you have high wages there will be higher prices and the spiral will start; you know the story which is generally told. We say it is not necessary if you have higher wages to have higher prices, because there has been a great improvement in technical development in this country and also in the skill of the people who operate the machines. Further, there is plenty of surplus profits which could be used without impoverishing a single employer. The statistical summary published by the Bank of Canada reveals that 'profits of Canadian businesses in 1944, after allowing all deductions for taxes, were $416 million, or nearly double what they were in 1936. The same survey states that the accumulated surplus and surplus reserves of 700 companies in 1943 amounted to SI,188 million, compared with $800 million in 1938. So that therp is plenty of room right there for an increase in wages to give purchasing power to the people. It is not enough to give a man a job. The Minister of Reconstruction said a few months ago that there will be a million jobs. Yes, but unless they are jobs at decent wages we shall not have lasting prosperity. The less the purchasing power, the sooner a crash is bound to come. These are plain and simple facts of economics, and they demonstrate why- it is necessary that the wages paid to workers should be adequate.
A word as to the problem of unemployment insurance benefits. Let me point out that $14 or $10 will not make it possible for workers and their families to exist. The present unemployment insurance benefits are quite insufficient. Recently there was a Gallup poll, taken among all types of the population of Canada, in which forty-three per cent agreed that it is necessary to have increased unemployment insurance. Unless a man gets a reasonable unemployment benefit he will be forced to grab a job at low wages. Of course some people do not mind that, in fact it is just up their alley, but as far as the people who have to take these jobs at low wages are concerned, that is not so and the nation as a whole suffers as the result of such a policy. That is why increased unemployment insurance benefits are needed.
I would emphasize that these are things which have to be done. Fine words will not give the people of Canada what they need. Fine words will not fulfil the promises which were made to the men who went overseas to fight and are confronted with the problem to-day of finding a decent job. Fine words
Demobilization-Labour

will solve nothing. What is needed is bolder action by this government, and, particularly by the Department of Labour, and I hope that such action will be taken in order to avoid strikes. Nobody wants strikes if matters can be settled otherwise.
I was not going to say anything about the Japanese problem, but I feel that some remarks on my part will be in order at this time. It is always dangerous when you start "picking against" one group. When it is suggested that some one group is different, and that the people of that group just cannot become Canadians, the next thing we may expect will be attacks upon another group, and'then upon another. Maybe the next time it will be the Italians, or perhaps the Jews. It so happens that I am unable to see what is supposed to make these people so terribly different. I cannot understand why they should be discriminated against as compared with Germans or Italians. Why are the Germans treated differently from the Japanese? Surely the Germans in this country, or at any rate some of them, were as active on behalf of nazi Germany as wTere the Japanese on behalf of Japan, yet nobody would suggest that the Germans should be deported. Is it because of a difference in colour? It is dangerous to start differentiating against any race because of its colour. That is exactly the ideology against which we fought in this war. Speaking on this matter last year, I pointed out, and I want to repeat it to-day, that if we wish to make sure that the Japanese will constitute no problem, no threat to this country, let us eradicate militarism and shintoism, and everything which is rotten in Japan. Let them stand up and say that they do not want the emperor to remain on his job. Let them say that they want to break up the feudal system and take away the land from the wealthy landowners, those who plotted the war, and give it to the people. Give them a real taste of democracy. Let them uproot what is rotten in Japanese life, and the Japanese people here will constitute no problem. It is always bad to treat a problem superficially. That is true of the Japanese question and it is also true of labour relations: we have to get down to the basic issues confronting the people here and elsewhere. Only then shall we be in a position to make solutions which will be in the best interests of the people.

I have some difficulty in following the previous speaker. He has an advantage over me: he is the whip, the leader and the critic of his party. But I suggest that possibly he should have stayed with the subject upon which he started at

first, because he may know something about that, and certainly he knows nothing about the Japanese problem.

May I tell the hon. member that I went out in 193S to Vancouver to give information to the people of that city about Japanese espionage, but I could not get it over the air because the Japanese consul had so much power in Vancouver.

The hon. member might be able to give the people of Vancouver some information, but as to the rest of us in British Columbia, I do not. think he can give us information on the Japanese. Upon one point I quite agree with him; that is, when he says that we should assist Japan to gc-t rid of her present system; and if he will come up to my district when he is again in our province, I will see that he gets half an hour on the radio free. When he says that some things could be done to solve the problem by educating Japan, I certainly agree with him. If we want to wipe out imperialism and shintoism I agree that the best way to do so is to educate them. I say to the hon. member for Cartier and to the members of the group immediately opposite me that I think Canadians have done very well in the past in sending missionaries to all these countries which practice cannibalism and every other kind of ism, to try to convert them to democratic ideas. But I also say to my hon. friends across the way, would they tell me any way which would be easier, quicker and cheaper to get 29,000 missionaries to teach Canada's democratic way of life than by sending the Japanese back to Japan to tell their friends about it? I do not think there is any better way. I do not believe that the members of the Liberal and Conservative parties generally wanted to get into this debate, and certainly I had no intention of doing so until I heard what in my opinion was one of the most racial speeches ever delivered in this house since I have been here. That speech was delivered by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I should think any party that claims to have the interests of labour at heart, especially under present conditions, when we read the headlines in the newspapers and think of the struggle that is going on among the ranks of labour, would have addressed itself to the problems of labour instead of discussing the subject that has been brought up. But so far only two members of that party have tried to contribute anything to the welfare of labour, at least as far as I can see. One of them is the hon. member

Demobilization-Labour
for Qu'Appelle and the other the hon. member for Cape Breton South, who always earnestly, conscientiously, and I think brilliantly, defends labour.
But we did not get any contribution of that kind from the hon. member for Vancouver East. I can understand the position of the members of that party, however, and even the position of the Progressive Conservative party. They are not very strong-
They are getting better all the time.

You need to get a good deal better. However, I would say to the Liberals and the Conservatives that perhaps we should adopt something of the policy of the C.C.F. and prepare for the future, because there will be elections coming on again not only in four years' time but in eight years, twelve years, sixteen years and so on. Possibly one of the reasons my friends of the C.C.F. are planning their programme as they are is this very fact. At least, according to the Vancouver Daily Province, a responsible newspaper, they may be looking to the future for votes, because I see by the Province of October 4, 1944, the headline, "Possible solution to Jap problem; C.C.F. suggests intermarriage." Maybe that is the solution for the future from the point of view of votes. The newspaper io which I am referring gives a report of a meeting, and I see that at that meeting a suggestion was made which perhaps proposes one way in which they might be able to get a class of voters who would endorse some of their policies. One speaker at that meeting suggested:
If one hundred o-f the best white boys were married to one hundred of the best Japanese girls they would have a product Canada would be proud of.
What a suggestion!
Who said that?

A C.C.F. speaker at a C.C.F. meeting in the city of Vancouver. That may be one way of getting satisfactory voters in the future, and it may be one reason why in Saskatchewan only two of the Japanese have been asked to be sent back to Japan. I do not know.
I almost wept last night when the hon. member for Vancouver East told us about the old Japanese father. I am not trying in any way to poke fun at this poor old Japanese father, because I admire any father, of any race, who expresses a wish to see his son before he dies. But, as I say, I almost wept when the hon. gentleman, told us of this dear old Japanese in British Columbia who before his death was so anxious to have his son visit him
and who was unfortunately comforted only by the return of his daughter. Well, I thought of some of the mothers in my own riding who to-day have not yet got Their sons back from Hong Kong because those boys are in hospitals. I thought of other mothers in my riding whose sons will never return, and then I did not weep so much.
I am not. one of those who are afraid to speak of atrocities when we hear all this claptrap about such dear, delightful Japanese men who are so loyal to Canada and! who must not be sent back. I heard the leader of the C.C.F. party, perhaps rightly, defend the league of nations, but I would like him to check up on some of the -actions of the. league of nations after the last war when they moved hundreds of thousands of Greeks, Turks and Armenians from their own native land. I have not heard so much from my hon. friends of the C.C.F. about Russia whose system they so proudly boast of. Perhaps I am treading on dangerous ground when I talk about international affairs, but I have not heard so much about those people who were taken from Poland, from their own country, and moved elsewhere. Not a word about them.-
I should like to say a word with reference to my friend the hon. member for Koptenay West, because he is a good friend of mine. He has the advantage of rooming next door to me. -He is something like the hon. member for Cartier, because he is in a sort of no-man's land, in a party of his own. He has the- great advantage of having been a Liberal in the past, and I forgive him a good deal because I do not think he knows anything about the Japanese problem. If he is so anxious to have them in his riding there will be no quarrel in Fraser Valley should his wish be fulfilled. I would point out, however, that prior to Pearl Harbor and the evacuation of the Japanese from the coast, there was exactly one Jap in his riding. I also had some of those letters from people in -his riding, from the ghost towns where merchants were bankrupt until, the Japs moved in. I had letters from certain organizations. I can understand the interior saw mills wanting cheap Jap labour, but I do not understand the remarks we have heard, from people with reference to that terrible word, not leprosy, but capitalism. Let me quote something from the Vancouver Sun-if you can quote from two good papers like these, you will get your name in both to-mo-rrow. I quote the following:
We, the undersigned Canadian-born Japanese
I have not the time to read the whole of this article, but I want the committee to mark

Demobilization-Labour
those words, "Canadian-born Japanese". A little further on they are referred to as "loyal and patriotic Japanese", and further on still:
... we Japanese people regard our imperial family as divine and whose sanctity is inviolable. A recent editorial in the Vancouver Sun, unjustly condemning the peaeedoving imperial Japanese of militarism . . .
This is from Japanese, and I can give their signatures if necessary. I quote again:
If the Canadian public in general had kept their eyes open during the recent visit of Prince and Princess Chichihu they would have observed that no Japanese looked down on the august procession of their imperial highnesses from the windows above, so great is our respect for the divine persons of our imperial family.
This is from loyal Canadian Japanese.
That no objection was made-
Mark that.
-to Canadians- and other foreigners from doing so was merely a concession on the part of the Japanese people concerning those who do not as yet fully -appreciate their highly patriotic feelings.
Lower down I read:
We Japanese are a proud and sensitive people, and the imperial Japanese empire has a way of dealing' with those people and nations who show their insincerity by disregarding and flouting our most sacred sentiments and feelings.
A threat of what they would have done to us! I do not want to go into details. The hon. member for Vancouver South and the hon. member for New Westminster have given the opinion of the people of British Columbia, supported !by vote a short time ago in the provincial election, when the most influential members of the C.C.F. party in British Columbia fell by the wayside, including one who, as the hon. member for Vancouver East knows better than I do, has two-thirds of the brains of the C.C.F. party in that province. Unfortunately she fell by the wayside in that election. Why? Because the people of British Columbia do not and-I impress this upon the government-will not allow the return of the Japanese.
I wish to say one thing to the government and I absolutely agree in this with the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member for Vancouver South; when you get south and east together, Fraser Valley can get in the middle It is time for the government to state what they are going to do about this agreement. Only two members from eastern Canada have told me they disagree with our stand on the Japanese question,, and those two were from Ontario. I should like to ask them a question. I am not going to look at them because I do not want their ' constituents to know to whom I am referring, but they sit over there. Only two members

said that they would like the Japanese in their district. I am going to suggest to the premier from my own province that when he comes to the conference on the 26th, he use as one of the bargaining powers, before he makes -any further concessions to Quebec or Ontario, a demand from the Prime Minister of Canada an official and final stand as to where Canada stands on the Japanese question. It is time we did that. We are not trying to wish them on you people; we think they should go back to Japan, but we are definitely saying it is a federal and dominion responsibility now and you people must accept your responsibility on the matter. If you do not want them here that is your privilege, but when the Minister of Labour says that we have no agreement with the province of Quebec, and when we remember that the province of Quebec has one-third of the population of Canada and only 671 Japanese, it is time that something was done.
On the elevator last night one hon. member from New Brunswick asked me what a Japanese looked like. He said that he had never seen one in his life. It is time they had a few there. You do not want them; that is the point. Then, see that we do not get them. The city of Toronto has a larger population than the whole province of British Columbia. They refuse to accept them; yet I am asked to go back to the taxpayers of British Columbia, who do not get paid federal money on federally owned land, and justify why we spend hundreds and hundreds of thousands of dollars in trying to beautify this town. If you spent ten million dollars you would still only have the parliament buildings. Karsh and some bad restaurants. I am not objecting to spending that money, but when I find the capital of Canada will not accept anjr of their share, then I say we from British Columbia are justified in asking private members from all parts of the Dominion of Canada to stand by us.
We do not approach the matter from the racial hatred point of view; we have none for the Japanese. Hon. members may think it is racial hatred, but we put up with some of the rest of you people in Canada. We are asking you people to take your own fair share of the problem; we shall take ours, if needs be.
I should like to say this: Probably for the first time in the history of British Columbia are, not one hundred per cent-I will not say that-but in spite of the C.C.F., at least ninety-four per cent unanimous on this problem. Do not think for one minute that every person who voted for the C.C.F. party in British Columbia is in favour of their stand on the Japanese question. I know they are

Demobilization-Labour
not and the C.C.F. members know they are not. There are too many fine men and women in British Columbia who belong to the C.C.F. party to endorse any such ridiculous attitude as that. We know that we have ninety-four per cent of the people of British Columbia behind us. We British Columbia members, Liberals and Conservatives, are warning the government and the members of parliament that no longer will British Columbia be pushed around on the Japanese problem.
